source.publisher: Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources, Government of Türkiye

records.limits: The ministry page establishes the contract, capacity, factory and R&D milestones and the later cancellation, but it does not publish the cancellation cost, foregone generation or the reasons for the legislative change. Counting two completed facilities is a direct count of the page's milestones, not an independent audit of their operation; cancellation is evidence about delivery durability rather than renewable output.

pattern.mechanism: The state tied a renewable auction to domestic manufacturing and research obligations, then later used a statutory change to cancel the contract despite preparatory industrial facilities having been completed.
preconditions: A ministry able to bundle generation rights with local-content obligations
Private consortia willing to build manufacturing and R&D capacity ahead of generation
Legislative authority able to reopen or cancel a signed concession
pattern.travelled: Industrial-policy tenders travel only when contract stability is part of the bargain; a local factory does not rescue a project whose legal foundation can be rewritten midstream.

records.title: TÜBİTAK 1505 university–industry support programme
records.claim: TÜBİTAK's 1505 University–Industry Collaboration Support Programme received 116 project applications and began support for 59 projects in 2024, with 52 fellows working across the collaboration pipeline.

metric.name: Projects entering the support process

secondMetric.name: Project applications received

source.publisher: Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TÜBİTAK), 2024 activity report

records.limits: Applications and support starts measure the interface, not the number of products commercialised or the durability of university–firm relationships. The activity report is an administrative source and does not identify the firms, project quality or completion rate; 52 fellows are a staffing input, not an outcome.

pattern.mechanism: TÜBİTAK made firms' needs the entry point for university research, with a public grant and named academic and customer organisations sharing the project rather than leaving technology transfer to informal contacts.
preconditions: A public research fund able to contract with both universities and firms
Academic teams with usable research and firms willing to specify a problem
A review and reporting process that keeps the two sides accountable to one project plan
pattern.travelled: University–industry programmes travel when the firm is a real customer and the grant funds a jointly owned deliverable; a networking event without a project contract is not collaboration capacity.

records.title: Gotthard Base Tunnel
records.claim: Switzerland built the 57 km Gotthard Base Tunnel under the voter-approved NEAT programme and opened it to commercial traffic on 11 December 2016, on the date set, at a final cost forecast of CHF 9.541 billion against a 1998 cost basis of CHF 6.323 billion, both in 1998 prices.

metric.name: Cost growth against the 1998 cost basis, Gotthard axis including connections

secondMetric.name: Commercial opening against the scheduled timetable change

source.publisher: Swiss Federal Assembly, NEAT supervisory delegation (NAD), report on the oversight of NEAT construction in 2016, BBl 2017 5413

records.limits: The 51 percent is computed from the NAD's Table 2 (6,323 to 9,541 million francs, 1998 prices) and is not a headline the publisher states. That column mixes true overrun with scope added after 1998, including extra safety works and the Sedrun geology, so a like-for-like overrun would be lower. The cost basis is in real 1998 francs; the nominal bill, about CHF 12.2 billion with inflation, VAT and interest according to the Federal Office of Transport, is larger. On schedule means against the timetable fixed late in the project, which the NAD calls on time, not against the opening years implied by the 1992 vote. The started year is the 1998 financing vote; main construction contracts followed. The source is a PDF and the figures sit in Table 2 and section 1.8.

pattern.mechanism: Voters approved the programme and a ring-fenced rail fund, parliament set a total credit and a standing supervisory delegation that reports every year, and a single-purpose federal subsidiary, AlpTransit Gotthard, built it under that oversight.
preconditions: Direct democracy that ties a ring-fenced fund to one programme
A standing parliamentary delegation that publishes cost forecasts every year
Tunnelling and rail engineering capacity already in the country
pattern.travelled: The Brenner and Mont Cenis base tunnels copy the engineering but run across two states with EU co-financing, and both have moved their opening dates repeatedly.

records.title: Civil defence shelters
records.claim: Finland requires a shelter in every building above a size threshold, nationwide since 1991, and by 2023 had about 50,500 shelters with places for about 4.8 million people, in a country of about 5.6 million.

metric.name: Civil defence shelter places

secondMetric.name: Civil defence shelters

source.publisher: Finnish Government, Ministry of the Interior

records.limits: Both numbers are rounded by the ministry, which says the decades-long history makes precise register data hard to compile. Places are unevenly spread: the same release puts Helsinki at 34 percent more places than residents and South Ostrobothnia at places for 48 percent of its population, so the national figure overstates rural protection. A place is a built room, not a tested capability; the ministry's later condition review found most shelters in good order but some equipment needing maintenance. Shelters protect against attack and hazardous releases and say little about recovery from floods or pandemics, which the indicator also asks about. 1991 is when the duty became nationwide; designated municipalities built shelters for decades before.

pattern.mechanism: The state put the cost of protection on construction itself: the Rescue Act obliges owners of large residential and workplace buildings to build a shelter, which peacetime uses as storage, car parks or sports halls on condition it can be cleared within 72 hours.
preconditions: A threat perception shared across parties since the Second World War
A building code and permit inspection that enforce the duty before construction
Housing built mostly as concrete multi-storey blocks
pattern.travelled: Switzerland runs the same building duty. Germany and Sweden let theirs lapse after 1990 and are now rebuilding from a smaller stock.

records.title: Public civil defence shelters, and their dismantling
records.claim: Germany held 1,967 public shelters with about 1.6 million places in 2008, decided with the states to abandon them, and decommissioned them until March 2022, leaving 579 shelters with 477,593 places, none of them functional or operational.

metric.name: Public shelter places still designated

secondMetric.name: Public shelter places at the start of the run-down

source.publisher: German Federal Government, answer to a parliamentary question, Bundestag Drucksache 20/14631, figures from the Federal Institute for Real Estate (BImA)

records.limits: The 2008 figure is rounded by the government and covers only the western states and Berlin: shelters of the former GDR never entered the federal concept, so the stock was never national. Shelter places are an old measure of protection, and the government now argues bunkers cannot meet modern warning times and plans to rely on basements, car parks and metro stations, so the loss of places overstates the loss of preparedness if that concept is delivered. It had not been when this answer was given. The started year is the 1965 Shelter Construction Act; the federal funding programme for public shelters ran from 1968 to 1996. The source is a PDF; the numbers are in the answers to questions one and seven.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government and the states read the end of the Cold War as the end of the threat, stopped maintenance and budgeted to decommission and release the shelters, until the interior ministry froze the process by decree three weeks after Russia invaded Ukraine.
preconditions: A peace dividend read as permanent across parties
Shelters owned federally but sited in municipalities with other uses for the land
No statutory floor on protection places that a budget line could not override
pattern.travelled: Sweden and the Baltic states ran down civil defence in the same years and began rebuilding after 2014; Finland and Switzerland kept their building duty and are the comparators the German debate now cites.

records.title: Banco Central regulatory sandbox, first cycle
records.claim: Brazil's central bank opened its regulatory sandbox to applications in February 2021, received 52 projects, admitted seven to test under relaxed rules from 6 December 2021, and ran the cycle for one year with one permitted extension.

metric.name: Projects admitted to the first cycle

secondMetric.name: Projects that applied to the first cycle

source.publisher: Banco Central do Brasil, Relatório de Gestão do Sandbox Regulatório, 1º ciclo 2022

records.limits: The central bank is reporting on its own programme. Seven admissions out of 52 shows a selective regime, not a broad one: the report records that the bank found 24 projects not innovative enough or not needing any rule relief, judged five outside its remit, and disqualified 16 more. The report covers the first cycle only and says nothing about what the seven tests changed in regulation or which products reached the market. No second cycle appears in the bank's published sandbox documents as of the retrieval date, so the status is concluded on that absence, not on a closing statement. The securities regulator CVM runs a separate sandbox that this record does not count. The source is a PDF and the counts are on page 11.

pattern.mechanism: The National Monetary Council and the central bank set a joint sandbox rule in 2020, and a standing committee of seven department heads screened applications by cycle, admitting only projects that needed a specific rule relaxed to be tested.
preconditions: A central bank that already runs the payment rails it is willing to test against, as Pix shows
A legal basis that lets the regulator waive its own rules for a limited period
Enough supervisory staff to take on a cycle of bespoke oversight
pattern.travelled: The design follows the UK model of time-bound cohorts. Brazil kept the cohort small and the entry test strict, which limits both the risk and the reach.

records.title: Reserve Bank of India regulatory sandbox
records.claim: The Reserve Bank of India ran four themed sandbox cohorts between 2020 and 2024, retail payments, cross-border payments, MSME lending and fraud prevention, admitting 28 entities to test and finding 13 products viable in the three cohorts whose exits it published, and keeps the cohorts open on tap.

metric.name: Entities admitted to the test phase across four cohorts

secondMetric.name: Products found viable in the first, second and fourth cohorts

source.publisher: Reserve Bank of India, press release on the exit of the fourth Regulatory Sandbox cohort, 18 June 2024

records.limits: Both numbers are computed from four RBI press releases, not stated in one: six entities admitted and six viable in the first cohort (13 September 2021), eight and four in the second (19 July 2022), eight admitted to the third (6 June 2022) and six admitted with three viable in the fourth (18 June 2024). The third cohort's exit result was not found, so the viable count leaves it out. The regulator is reporting on its own programme, and viable within the boundary conditions of a test is not adoption: the releases say only that regulated entities may consider the products. Twenty-eight entities over four years is small next to India's payments sector, so the record evidences that a working sandbox exists, not that it shaped the market.

pattern.mechanism: The RBI published an enabling framework in 2019 and ran the sandbox as themed cohorts, each opened on one policy problem, so the regulator chose the questions and firms competed to answer them; a closed cohort reopens on tap.
preconditions: A central bank that sets policy for a fast-growing digital payments system it also oversees
Willingness to publish names of admitted entities and test outcomes
A pipeline of startups and incumbents with products held back by a specific rule
pattern.travelled: Themed cohorts are the RBI's variation on the UK model. The theme concentrates supervisory attention but caps volume, which is why the counts stay in single digits per cohort.

records.title: Seawater desalination under private concessions
records.claim: Israel's Water Authority contracted private operators to build and run large seawater desalination plants under long-term concessions, and by 2022 the five largest held concessions for about 596 million cubic metres a year and supplied 33 percent of the country's fresh water, with the state buying 540 million cubic metres from them that year for about NIS 1.5 billion.

metric.name: Share of fresh water supplied from desalination

secondMetric.name: Production capacity in the concessions of the five largest plants

source.publisher: State Comptroller of Israel, Regulation and Oversight of Seawater Desalination Facilities, November 2024

records.limits: The source is an audit, and most of it is criticism: it finds that the Water Authority never completed the national desalination master plan a 2010 government resolution required, that the agreed penalties for poor water quality are too low to enforce anything, that 14 seawater contamination incidents halted production between 2007 and 2023, that three of the largest plants sit near one river mouth, and that no serious preparation had begun for the Palmachim concession expiring in 2029. A third of fresh water is the 2022 national share; desalination's share of drinking water is higher, but the audit does not state it. The started year is the first year the audit reports plants in operation; the first plant opened earlier. Capacity is a contractual figure, not output.

pattern.mechanism: The state kept the planning, the water purchase and the regulation, and let private consortia finance, build and operate each plant on a long-term concession with a guaranteed buyer, so capacity arrived on a tender schedule without the capital sitting on the budget.
preconditions: A single national water authority and a national carrier able to take every plant's output
A coastline next to the demand and enough grid power for reverse osmosis
Water scarcity severe and lasting enough to sustain the political case across governments
pattern.travelled: Gulf states and Australia built similar plants; where demand fell after a drought ended, as in several Australian cities, plants were mothballed and the fixed concession payments became the controversy.

records.title: Kenya's adult education centres, and their halving
records.claim: Kenya's state adult education programme, run since the 1978 presidential literacy decree through adult education centres in every county, enrolled 330,340 learners in 2014 and 165,552 in 2025, after a low of 125,402 in 2023, according to the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in adult education centres

secondMetric.name: Learners enrolled in adult education centres at the 2014 peak of the published series

source.publisher: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, Economic Survey 2026, Table 15.27 (source: State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizens Affairs, Directorate of Adult Learning and Education)

records.limits: The metric is a head count of learners in adult education centres, mostly basic literacy, not the share of adults in formal or non-formal education and training that the indicator defines: 165,552 is well under one percent of Kenya's adult population, and the count leaves out TVET, university, employer training and private courses entirely. The peak is only the highest year in the series KNBS publishes from 2010 onwards (252,553 in 2010, 330,340 in 2014). The 1980s literacy campaign almost certainly enrolled more, so the true loss from the programme's peak is understated, not overstated. The series is administrative and badly maintained. KNBS revised 2015 from 246,215 (Economic Survey 2016) to 306,228 (Economic Survey 2018). The 2025 figure is provisional. Several counties report identical numbers in consecutive years (Garissa 3,256 in all four years 2022 to 2025, and Samburu and Laikipia repeated), which points to carried-forward returns. One county, Nairobi, accounts for most of the 2025 rebound, rising from 13,194 to 34,506 in one year. Falling enrolment can partly reflect success, since younger cohorts went through universal primary schooling and need less remedial literacy, so the decline is evidence of lost provision only alongside the fact that the programme was reorganised across ministries and is now run by a social protection directorate. The 1978 start year is the presidential decree reported by the state news agency, not a documented first enrolment. The 2014 peak was itself revised: Economic Survey 2015 published 300,462 (provisional) and Economic Survey 2017 restated it as 330,340; against the earlier figure the fall to 2025 is about 45 percent rather than half.

pattern.mechanism: The presidency decreed a national literacy programme, and the education ministry, and later a social protection directorate, ran it through state-paid instructors in community adult education centres in every district. Enrolment fell by half over a decade as the function moved between ministries and county returns degraded.
preconditions: A large adult population that had missed primary school
A ministry department with paid instructors at district level
A political mandate that framed literacy as a national campaign rather than a welfare service

records.title: Capital Markets Authority regulatory sandbox
records.claim: Kenya's Capital Markets Authority opened a regulatory sandbox under a 2019 policy guidance note and by January 2024 had let 11 firms exit it after live testing, with new admissions continuing into January 2025.

metric.name: Firms that successfully exited the CMA regulatory sandbox

source.publisher: Capital Markets Authority of Kenya, press release 'CMA graduates Sycamore Capital Limited from the Regulatory Sandbox'

records.limits: This is one regulator's sandbox for capital markets products only. It says nothing about the Central Bank of Kenya, the Communications Authority or any other regulator, so it covers little of the breadth the indicator asks for. The count is the regulator's own, taken from a press release, and the CMA publishes no running register. The 11 exits are cumulative over almost five years, a small number that says nothing about what the exiting products did in the market. 'Successful exit' is the CMA's own description. The figure is from January 2024, and no later official total was found.

pattern.mechanism: The Capital Markets Authority issued a policy guidance note that let fintech firms and incumbents test capital markets products with real customers under relaxed rules, then used each exit as the moment to grant a licence or approval under the Capital Markets Act.
preconditions: A regulator with statutory power to grant no-objections and tailored approvals
A domestic fintech sector already built on mobile money rails
Peer regulators abroad, through the Global Financial Innovation Network, to copy procedures from

records.title: Standard Gauge Railway, Mombasa to Naivasha
records.claim: Kenya Railways began building the Standard Gauge Railway in financial year 2014/15, completed the 472 km Mombasa to Nairobi Phase I in 2017, and opened the 120 km Phase 2A to Naivasha in September 2019 against a September 2017 start and an 18-month plan, about six months late; the line hauled 7.33 million tonnes of freight in 2025.

metric.name: Planned construction period of SGR Phase 2A (Sept 2017 start, KSh 155.5 billion), against which the line opened in September 2019, about six months (a third) late

secondMetric.name: Freight hauled on the SGR

source.publisher: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, Economic Survey 2018

records.limits: No official source found publishes the outturn cost of either phase against its budget, so the record carries a cost plan (KSh 155.5 billion for Phase 2A) and no cost performance. That is the half of the construct that matters most for a Chinese-financed turnkey contract. The schedule overrun of about six months on Phase 2A, or a third of the 18-month plan, is computed: the plan is from KNBS, and the opening is from the Ministry of Roads and Transport Strategic Plan 2023-2027 draft ('completed Phase 2A ... and was launched for operation in September 2019', https://www.transport.go.ke/sites/default/files/DRAFT%20FINAL%20MINISTERIAL%20STRATEGIC%20PLAN%202023-27%20FEB%202024%20.pdf). Phase I's schedule against its plan cannot be checked from an official copy. The National Assembly's 2014 Public Investments Committee report giving a December 2016 completion date and a USD 3.804 billion contract price was found only on an NGO mirror. The parliamentary repository timed out, so neither figure is used. The railway was meant to run to Malaba and into Uganda, and the Naivasha to Malaba section remained unbuilt for years. The same ministry plan reports rail carrying 19 percent of port throughput in 2021 against a 50 percent target for 2030. Freight tonnage is published by KNBS from Kenya Railways returns. Debt service and fiscal cost are not shown at all.

pattern.mechanism: The Treasury and Kenya Railways contracted a Chinese state contractor on a design-build-supply basis with Exim Bank finance, which put construction risk and speed on the contractor and left financing, land acquisition and traffic risk with the state.
preconditions: A bilateral lender willing to finance most of the cost against sovereign guarantees
A state able to acquire a 472 km corridor of land quickly
A port whose cargo the state could steer onto rail to fill the line

records.title: Rwanda's adult literacy centres, and their decline
records.claim: Rwanda's Ministry of Education reports 93,548 learners in adult literacy centres in 2024/25, down from 152,015 in 2017.

metric.name: Learners in adult literacy centres

secondMetric.name: Learners in adult literacy centres at the 2017 high of the five-year table

source.publisher: Rwanda Ministry of Education, 2024/2025 Education Statistical Yearbook (school census)

records.limits: The start year is weak. 2003 is the sector policy that committed the state to adult literacy training, not a documented first enrolment, and adult literacy classes ran before it. A reviewer could fairly set the year elsewhere. The programme never came near its own targets: the 2003 policy implied about 500,000 learners a year. The '2017 peak' is only the high of one published five-year table, and earlier years were not checked. Delivery is mixed: the yearbooks blame part of the decline on NGOs and projects closing and on religious buildings ceasing to host centres. Some of the loss is therefore civil society withdrawing rather than the state, even though the ministry counts and partly funds all centres. The 2024/25 yearbook states the latest fall as 5.8 percent in one place and 5.7 percent in another. A head count of literacy learners is far narrower than the share of adults in any education or training that the indicator defines.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Education set national literacy targets and counted learners through its school census, but relied on churches, NGOs and donor projects to host and staff most centres. When those partners withdrew, enrolment fell, and no state budget line replaced them.
preconditions: A national school census that reaches non-formal centres
Religious and NGO networks willing to host classes in every sector
Public funding for instructors that would hold up when donor projects ended, which is the precondition that failed here

records.title: Government of Rwanda and Zipline drone delivery network
records.claim: From 2016 the Government of Rwanda contracted Zipline to fly blood and later other medical products to health facilities, and by 2024 the Rwanda Biomedical Centre reported deliveries to 624 sites across 27 districts and over 12,000 packages in a single month.

metric.name: Delivery sites served by drone

secondMetric.name: Packages delivered in a single month

source.publisher: Rwanda Biomedical Centre, Head of the Blood Transfusion Service, 'Revolutionizing Rwanda's Supply Chain: The Impact of UAVs (2016-2023)', presented at the ICAO Advanced Air Mobility Symposium 2024 and hosted by ICAO

records.limits: The source is a slide deck by the public partner, presented at an aviation conference. It is not a statistical release, and its operating figures almost certainly come from Zipline, the private contractor, so the number is the two partners reporting on themselves. 'Today' is undated beyond the 2024 symposium, and 'over 12,000 packages in a single month' is a lower bound for an unnamed month, not an annual series. The site count mixes health facilities with farms and other drop points, and 27 districts is not all 30. The deck's outcome claims (90 percent less wastage, 99 percent less maternal mortality from blood shortage) are unreferenced on the slide and are not used here. The record shows scale, not value for money: contract prices, per-delivery cost to the health budget, and whether road logistics would have done as well are not shown. The collaboration is with one foreign firm under a service contract, which is a narrow form of the joint public-private delivery the indicator means.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Health and the Rwanda Biomedical Centre bought a delivery service rather than drones: Zipline built and flew the network, the state paid per delivery, centralised the blood supply, and the civil aviation authority opened the airspace.
preconditions: A centralised national blood service able to stock regional hubs
An aviation regulator willing to authorise beyond-visual-line-of-sight flights at national scale
Health facilities with a reliable ordering channel and a government that pays per delivery
pattern.travelled: Zipline took the contract model to Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya and Côte d'Ivoire. Its durability has depended on each health ministry's ability to keep paying fees once donor co-funding ends.

records.title: Canadian long-gun registry, its information system overrun and its dismantling
records.claim: Canada began registering all firearms under the 1995 Firearms Act from December 1998. The registry's first information system, CFIS I, had an initial estimate of $13 to 20 million and had cost $190 million by March 2005. Its successor CFIS II rose from $32 million to at least $87 million and was halted. In 2012 Parliament ended long-gun registration and ordered the destruction of about 7.5 million non-restricted registration records, which the RCMP deleted from CFIS in October 2012.

metric.name: Cost of the Canadian Firearms Information System (CFIS I), against an initial estimate of $13 to 20 million

secondMetric.name: Non-restricted firearms registration records in CFIS when Parliament ordered their destruction

source.publisher: House of Commons of Canada, Standing Committee on Public Accounts, Report 10 (39th Parliament, 1st Session), on Chapter 4 of the May 2006 Report of the Auditor General, Canadian Firearms Program

records.limits: The cost figure is a Commons committee's summary of the Auditor General's 2006 follow-up. The Auditor General's own 2002 and 2006 chapters no longer open at their published OAG URLs, so the record rests on Parliament's restatement of them. The $190 million covers CFIS I, the information system, and is not the cost of the whole programme. The often quoted figure of roughly $1 billion for the programme could not be verified at an official URL today and is not used. The baseline is a range of $13 to 20 million given at an early stage, so any overrun ratio, roughly ten times, depends on which end is chosen and on how far the scope of that early estimate matched the system that was built. The committee itself attributes part of the growth to things outside the project team's control: requirements kept changing, and Bill C-10 and its regulations were delayed by more than two years. The dismantling in 2012 was a political decision by a new parliamentary majority. It was not a collapse caused by the delivery, so the status records a policy reversal rather than a technical failure. Licensing and the registry of restricted and prohibited firearms kept running, Quebec residents' records were held back pending litigation, and public agencies still register. The 7.5 million records show the scale the registry reached and say nothing about their accuracy, which the 2006 audit questioned. Like can-phoenix, this is a public IT system rather than physical infrastructure.

pattern.mechanism: The Department of Justice, and later the Canada Firearms Centre, built a universal national registry through contracted IT development while the regulations it had to implement were still changing, and reported the rising cost to ministers before Parliament. In 2012 Parliament ended the long-gun part by statute and had the RCMP destroy its records.
preconditions: Legislation and regulations settled before the system is specified, so requirements do not move during the build
Cost reporting to Parliament that covers the full programme, not only what is appropriated each year
A political settlement on registration durable enough to survive a change of government, or a design that does not depend on one

records.title: The 1997 Canada Pension Plan financing reform
records.claim: In December 1993 the Chief Actuary projected that the pay-as-you-go contribution rate would reach 14.2% by 2030 and that the fund would run out by 2015. The federal and provincial governments agreed a reform package in 1997. It took effect on 1 January 1998, raised the combined contribution rate in steps to 9.9% by 2003, replaced pay-as-you-go financing with steady-state funding and invested net cash flows through the CPP Investment Board. The 2024 valuation puts the minimum sustaining rate at 9.19% from 2034, below the legislated 9.9%, with assets of $651 billion.

metric.name: Combined employee-employer base CPP contribution rate reached under the reform, legislated since 2003

secondMetric.name: Pay-as-you-go contribution rate projected for 2030 without reform (15th Actuarial Report, December 1993)

source.publisher: Office of the Chief Actuary, Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, Actuarial Report (32nd) on the Canada Pension Plan (revised version), valuation as at 31 December 2024

records.limits: The construct is speed, and this reform was not fast. Four years passed between the December 1993 warning and the amendments taking effect in January 1998, and the rate took until 2003 to reach 9.9%. Whether that counts as responsive depends on a comparison the record cannot supply: it shows a rule changed in time, before the projected 2015 exhaustion, and not that it changed quickly. The headline numbers are a legislated rate and a projection, not an observed outcome. The evidence that the reform held, a 9.19% minimum rate against 9.9%, is the Chief Actuary's model under his own assumptions. That office sits inside OSFI, so this is a federal body assessing a federal-provincial plan. The fix was paid for mostly by workers and employers through a contribution rate up about 70% from 1997, plus slower benefit growth, which a reader may count as a cost of the delay as much as a sign of capability. Quebec runs its own plan, so the CPP covers the rest of Canada. The amendment formula requires the agreement of provinces holding most of the population, and that slows any reform as well as stabilising it.

pattern.mechanism: The Chief Actuary's statutory triennial reports put a dated number on the funding gap. Federal and provincial finance ministers then negotiated one package that raised contributions, trimmed benefit growth and moved new money into market investment under an arm's-length board, and wrote into the statute that any future benefit increase must be fully funded.
preconditions: An actuarial office whose projections both orders of government accept as the shared baseline
A joint amendment rule that forces federal and provincial governments into one negotiated package
Enough time before the projected exhaustion date to phase in a contribution rise
pattern.travelled: The 1997 package required any future benefit increase to be fully funded. The additional CPP in force since 1 January 2019 is fully funded, and the 32nd report sets its own minimum contribution rates on that basis.

records.title: Tel Aviv light rail Red Line
records.claim: Israel's government approved the Red Line in December 2010 at an estimated NIS 10.7 billion, and NTA, the state-owned company delivering it, began the main construction works in 2015. By October 2021 the cost estimate had reached NIS 18.71 billion, about 75% above the original, and the completion date had been postponed six times, by about five years in total. The 24 km line opened in August 2023, and in December 2025 the State Comptroller put its construction cost at NIS 18.8 billion.

metric.name: Increase in the Red Line cost estimate over the December 2010 government estimate of NIS 10.7 billion

secondMetric.name: Cumulative postponement of the Red Line completion date across six postponements

source.publisher: State Comptroller of Israel, The Progress of the Light Rail Project in the Tel Aviv Metropolitan Area, November 2022

records.limits: The 75% overrun is the audit's figure for the October 2021 estimate and includes indexation. Net of price-index linkage and a VAT cut, the audit puts the real increase at about NIS 7.46 billion, or 69.7%. The audit was finished before the line opened, so the overrun is measured on an estimate rather than a final account. The December 2025 audit's NIS 18.8 billion construction cost comes from a security audit and is not a reconciled final cost. The five-year delay counts slippage to the then target of 2022. The line actually opened in August 2023, about six years after the original 2017 date, so the figure understates the final schedule slip. Most postponements came before main construction began in 2015, so a hostile reader would call them planning slippage rather than construction delay. The project is national in its funding, its government resolution and its state-owned delivery company, but it serves one metropolitan area, and one line is a single case and not a national delivery record. The audit's per-kilometre comparisons with other cities are not used here. Ridership is not established: the 300,000 passengers a day in the 2025 audit is NTA's forecast. The audit also found the framework agreement between NTA and the finance and transport ministries still unsigned more than 20 years after the company was founded.

pattern.mechanism: The government set the budget and target date by resolution in 2010 and handed delivery to NTA, a state-owned company. NTA revised the cost estimate at least eight times and moved the opening date six times, most of them before main construction began, and still brought the line into service in 2023.
preconditions: A dedicated state delivery company with a signed framework agreement setting its accountability to the transport and finance ministries, which the audit found missing
Contingency budgets set by the transport projects procedure from the first estimate, rather than costs left out of early estimates
Land clearance and right of way secured before the main contracts are tendered

records.title: Dynamic zero-COVID containment, and its dismantling
records.claim: China's State Council joint prevention and control mechanism ran a national COVID-19 containment regime from January 2020, under which the mainland had reported 4,634 COVID-19 deaths when vaccination began on 15 December 2020; it dismantled the regime by circular on 7 December 2022, and the National Health Commission then reported 59,938 COVID-related deaths in medical institutions between 8 December 2022 and 12 January 2023.

metric.name: COVID-related deaths in medical institutions in the five weeks after the regime was dismantled

secondMetric.name: Cumulative reported COVID-19 deaths under containment, at the start of vaccination

source.publisher: Xinhua report of a National Health Commission press conference of the State Council joint COVID-19 prevention and control mechanism, published on the State Council portal (english.www.gov.cn)

records.limits: Both numbers are the government's own and both are made under counting rules that understate deaths: the 59,938 covers only deaths inside medical institutions, and independent estimates put excess deaths far above the official count, so the official figure is a floor, not the toll. The two metrics cover different periods, populations at risk and counting rules (a cumulative count over 11 months against a five-week in-hospital count), so their ratio is not a mortality comparison. The SCIO text carrying 4,634 is an advocacy piece republished by the State Council Information Office, not a statistical release. The record does not show the costs of containment itself (lockdowns, lost output, mental-health and access-to-care harms), which were part of why it ended, nor that the dismantling followed Omicron's transmissibility rather than a planned exit. What it shows about preparedness is the exit gap: the State Council portal reported on 30 November 2022 that only 65.8 percent of people aged 80 and over had completed primary vaccination (english.www.gov.cn/statecouncil/ministries/202211/30/content_WS6386aabec6d0a757729e3d55.html), a week before the regime was lifted, and 90.1 percent of the reported deaths were aged 65 and above. The construct fit is contestable: the record evidences a national shock-containment capacity and its abrupt removal, not a standing disaster-recovery system. No official series of excess mortality for 2022-2023 has been published that would let the reversal be sized properly.

pattern.mechanism: The State Council joint prevention and control mechanism used mass testing, health codes and area lockdowns to hold infections near zero for nearly three years, then withdrew the whole apparatus by one circular within weeks, before raising vaccination coverage among the oldest residents. The capacity to suppress was built; the capacity to exit was not prepared in parallel.
preconditions: A command structure able to impose testing, movement codes and lockdowns uniformly across provinces
A population and economy able to absorb repeated closures, which wore out by late 2022
An exit plan, above all high vaccination of the oldest cohorts and hospital surge capacity, which was missing when the regime was lifted
pattern.travelled: Other zero-COVID jurisdictions (New Zealand, Australia, Taiwan) exited after vaccinating their elderly first; the Chinese exit is the case where suppression ended before that precondition was met.

records.title: National high-speed rail network
records.claim: China's railway authorities built a high-speed rail network that the National Railway Administration put at about 47,000 km in operation in December 2024, from a programme that began in 2003; a World Bank review of the 27 lines in operation at the end of 2013 found a weighted average approved unit cost of RMB 129m per km for 350 km/h lines, which it put at no more than two-thirds of costs elsewhere.

metric.name: High-speed rail track in operation

secondMetric.name: Weighted average unit cost of 350 km/h lines, approved estimates, lines in operation at end 2013

source.publisher: Statement of the National Railway Administration of China reported by Xinhua, on the State Council portal (english.www.gov.cn)

records.limits: Neither number is the overrun this gap asks for. The World Bank unit cost is built from estimated cost at project approval, not out-turn cost, so it cannot show whether lines came in over or under budget; the note itself warns that the data exist only in aggregate, that expenditures fall in different years and may not be comparable, and that its inputs come from China Railway and former Ministry of Railways publications. It is a 2014 staff note in a working series, covering about 10,000 km built by 2013, not the 47,000 km now operating, and the World Bank lends to Chinese railway projects. The 47,000 km figure is a rounded administrative statement by the regulator, relayed by Xinhua on the State Council portal, not a statistical table. Neither source shows the financing side: the debt carried by China State Railway Group and its predecessor, the low traffic density on many later lines, or the 2011 Wenzhou collision and the corruption cases at the former Ministry of Railways. Low unit cost also reflects cheap labour and land acquisition terms that are not institutional choices other countries can copy. No schedule-performance figure was found at an official URL.

pattern.mechanism: The former Ministry of Railways and its successors standardised designs, viaduct and station types and procurement across a national programme, then built continuously for two decades, so each line reused the previous line's templates, supply chain and crews.
preconditions: A single national rail authority with power to plan corridors, acquire land and finance lines through state-owned debt
A continuous build pipeline long enough for standard designs and a domestic supply chain to pay off
Tolerance for debt and for low-traffic lines whose cost is carried off the general budget
pattern.travelled: Standardisation and a continuous pipeline are what the World Bank note offers as transferable; other countries that build one line at a time keep the high unit costs the note compares against.

records.title: Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant
records.claim: The UAE, through the Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation and under licences from the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation issued from 2010, built four APR-1400 reactors at Barakah that ENEC reported in September 2024 were all in commercial operation and providing up to 25 percent of the UAE's electricity; Unit 1 entered commercial operation on 6 April 2021, about four years after the 2017 date the regulator recorded in its 2012 construction licence review.

metric.name: Share of UAE electricity supplied by Barakah, all four units operating
metric.unit: % of UAE electricity (up to, as reported)

secondMetric.name: Unit 1 commercial operation delay against the 2012 licensing plan (computed: April 2021 against a planned 2017)

source.publisher: Abu Dhabi Government Media Office, release on Barakah Unit 4 commercial operation (statement of the Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation)

records.limits: The 25 percent is the operator reporting on itself, relayed by the Abu Dhabi government's media office, and it is phrased as "up to": it is a capacity claim, not a measured share of national generation in a given year, and no statistical series was opened to confirm it. The schedule figure is computed by us from two documents, a 2012 regulator statement that the first unit was planned for 2017 and the 2021 commercial-operation release; it is a slip of roughly four years for Unit 1 only, and the later units' original dates were not found at an official URL. The plant's construction cost, and any cost overrun, are not published in any source opened, so the cost half of the construct is missing. The reactors were designed and built by a KEPCO-led Korean consortium on the Shin-Kori 3 and 4 reference design, so the UAE's institutional contribution is commissioning, licensing, financing and operating, not engineering. ENEC is an Abu Dhabi entity and the plant sits in one emirate, though it supplies the national grid under federal regulation. The operator's own boast of "a 40 per cent improvement in schedule" from Unit 1 to Unit 4 measures operational readiness to commercial operation, not construction, and is not used here.

pattern.mechanism: The UAE federal government set a nuclear policy in 2008, created an independent regulator (FANR) and a single owner-developer (ENEC), and bought a proven reactor design with a turnkey contract, so the state managed one prime contractor against one reference plant rather than a first-of-a-kind design.
preconditions: A sovereign balance sheet able to finance a multi-unit plant over a decade of construction and delay
A regulator built from scratch with foreign technical support, credible enough to hold the schedule back when licensing required it
A vendor with a recent reference plant and an intact domestic supply chain willing to export it
pattern.travelled: The turnkey, reference-plant model is what newcomer states such as Saudi Arabia and Poland cite; the four-year first-unit slip shows the regulator and operator readiness, not the construction, set the pace.

records.title: Integrated Functional Adult Education, and its erosion
records.claim: Ethiopia's Ministry of Education rolled out Integrated Functional Adult Education nationally from 2010/11 and enrolled 6,903,065 adults in 2015/16, but its successor Adult Basic Education Program enrolled 1,392,635 adults in 2024/25, about a fifth of the peak.

metric.name: Adults enrolled in the Adult Basic Education Program

secondMetric.name: Adults enrolled in Integrated Functional Adult Education at the 2015/16 peak

source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Education of Ethiopia, EMIS and ICT Executive Office, Education Statistics Annual Abstract 2024/25 (2017 E.C.)

records.limits: The 2024/25 count excludes Amhara and Tigray, which reported nothing because of conflict, and Amhara alone held 43 percent of IFAE enrolment in 2015/16; removing Amhara and Tigray, both absent in 2024/25, from the 2015/16 peak still leaves 3,450,597 against 1,392,635 (2,038,631 with Education Light), a figure we computed from Table 6.2 of the 2015/16 abstract and the ministry does not publish. The two numbers are not one series: the two-year IFAE became a one-year Adult Basic Education programme, and the 2024/25 abstract reports a separate Education Light/Torch track of 645,996 adults, so total adult enrolment that year was 2,038,631. All figures are administrative enrolment reported by regional bureaus to the ministry, with no attendance, completion quality or literacy outcome attached, and enrolment is not the construct's share of adults in education and training. The 2024/25 abstract has no stable PDF URL: it downloads from a button on the ministry's annual abstract page, so a checker must download it there and read PDF pages 63 to 64, printed pages 54 to 55 (sections 5.2 and 5.3, Table 5.1). The 2015/16 figure comes from a separate abstract PDF. The 2024/25 abstract also reports that 13,015,641 adults completed or graduated from IFAL/ABE between 2016/17 and 2024/25, so a shrinking pool of illiterate adults is a competing explanation for part of the fall.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Education built a national adult literacy programme run through regional education bureaus and community learning centres, then let enrolment fall by most of its peak as the programme was restructured and conflict removed whole regions from reporting.
preconditions: Regional education bureaus and kebele-level centres able to recruit facilitators and enrol adults at scale
A national campaign target, here ESDP IV's goal to cut adult illiteracy, that kept enrolment a political priority
Peace and administrative reach across regions, which the Amhara and Tigray conflicts removed
pattern.travelled: Mass literacy campaigns travel as enrolment drives; the Ethiopian series shows the reach depends on keeping the delivery network funded and present after the campaign target lapses.

records.title: Nigeria's 2014 Ebola containment
records.claim: After an infected traveller brought Ebola virus into Lagos on 20 July 2014, Nigeria's government set up an emergency operations centre with WHO country office support, traced contacts in Lagos and Port Harcourt, and held the outbreak to 19 cases and 7 deaths before WHO declared the country free of transmission on 20 October 2014.

metric.name: Ebola cases in the Nigerian outbreak

secondMetric.name: Ebola deaths in the Nigerian outbreak

source.publisher: World Health Organization, One year into the Ebola epidemic: Successful Ebola responses in Nigeria, Senegal and Mali (January 2015)

records.limits: This is one outbreak seeded by a single imported chain in two cities, so it shows a response to one shock and not a standing national capacity. The page is a WHO narrative, not a dataset, and WHO and partners supported the response, which also leaned on emergency-operations staff, GPS tools and infrastructure and technologies in place for polio eradication, as the WHO page puts it. Nothing here shows Nigeria's performance in later shocks such as Lassa fever, cholera, floods or COVID-19, and a counterfactual of how far the virus would have spread is not measured.

pattern.mechanism: The Federal Ministry of Health and Lagos State stood up an emergency operations centre within days of confirmation, repurposed the polio programme's staff and GPS tracking for contact tracing, and funded isolation and treatment centres quickly.
preconditions: An existing surveillance and field workforce, here the polio eradication infrastructure, that could be redirected overnight
A domestic laboratory able to confirm the virus within days
Political authority to release emergency funds and coordinate federal and state agencies under one command
pattern.travelled: Nigeria's emergency operations centre model was formalised in the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and cited by WHO as the preparedness standard for at-risk countries; the transfer depends on having a pre-existing field programme to repurpose.

records.title: SEC Nigeria Regulatory Incubation Program
records.claim: Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission opened a one-year Regulatory Incubation sandbox in September 2023 and had admitted seven firms across cohorts 001/23 and 002/24 to test capital-market products, then cleared seven more entities into its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme in July 2026.

metric.name: Firms admitted to the Regulatory Incubation sandbox across two cohorts

secondMetric.name: Entities cleared for the Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme in one announcement

source.publisher: Securities and Exchange Commission, Nigeria, FinPort Registered FinTech Operators directory

records.limits: The count of seven is ours, read off the directory table as retrieved on 2026-10-01, which carries no publication date and may not be current; the SEC publishes no summary statistic, application count, graduation rate or outcome for any participant. Three of the seven RI firms (Trovotech, Wrapped CBDC, Blockvault) reappear among the seven ARIP admissions of July 2026, so the two metrics overlap and must not be added, and an ARIP Approval-in-Principle is by the SEC's own wording not a final licence. This is one regulator's sandbox in one sector: the Central Bank of Nigeria's separate sandbox framework is not counted, and the record says nothing about whether testing changed any rule.

pattern.mechanism: The SEC created a time-limited sandbox with conditional rule waivers and a year-long test period, then added an accelerated track to pull digital-asset firms that were operating informally into supervised testing.
preconditions: A regulator with statutory room to grant conditional waivers, here strengthened by the Investments and Securities Act 2025
A pipeline of fintech and digital-asset firms already serving Nigerian users outside the rules
Supervisory staff able to review participants and decide graduation or wind-down
pattern.travelled: Built on the FCA sandbox template; Nigeria's variant adds an accelerated track aimed at bringing crypto exchanges and tokenisation platforms already in the market under supervision, rather than only testing new products.

records.title: Empresa Energía Honduras loss-reduction partnership, and its reversal
records.claim: Honduras's state utility ENEE awarded Empresa Energía Honduras a public-private partnership contract in December 2015, with service starting in 2016, to run national distribution and cut technical and non-technical losses by 17%. Distribution losses fell from 33.38% to 27.11% by February 2018, rose to 35.37% by December 2020 and stood at 30.77% in December 2021. The state intervened the contract and took distribution back when it ended in August 2023.

metric.name: Electricity distribution losses, December 2021 (technical and non-technical)

secondMetric.name: Lowest distribution losses under the partnership (February 2018), the gain that was lost

source.publisher: Secretaría de Energía de Honduras, Dirección General de Electricidad y Mercados, Informe Estadístico Anual del Subsector Eléctrico Nacional 2021 (Tabla 11, from ENEE Subgerencia de Planificación y Gestión Comercial)

records.limits: The loss series is ENEE's own commercial accounting, republished by the Energy Secretariat under the government that intervened the contract and campaigned against it, so the source is not neutral. The table stops in December 2021. The 2022 and 2023 values, including the roughly 37 to 38 percent widely reported when the contract ended, appear only in press coverage, and this record does not carry them. The SEN text does not attribute the 2016 to 2018 fall to EEH by name. The 2020 rise coincides with COVID-19 lockdowns and hurricanes Eta and Iota, so not all of the reversal can be laid on the operator. The contract was intervened and then expired at the end of its term in August 2023. It was not cancelled outright, and 'dismantled' here means the partnership model ended and ENEE took distribution back, not that a court annulled it. The SAPP fact sheet has copy errors: a malformed start date, and a repayment source copied from an airport sheet ('COBROS POR SERVICIOS AEROPORTUARIOS'). The 17% target comes from SAPP's project description, not from the contract text. A loss percentage measures the outcome of the partnership and says nothing directly about how deep the collaboration was. It is evidence that a structured government-firm arrangement on a national goal was tried at national scale and failed, not a measure of collaboration.

pattern.mechanism: ENEE, through a Congress-approved PPP trust supervised by SAPP and an external supervisor, handed national distribution and loss recovery to a private operator paid from distribution revenue. When losses rose, the state intervened the contract and then let it lapse, moving loss recovery into its own Programa Nacional para la Reducción de Pérdidas.
preconditions: A loss baseline and metering both parties accept, so the operator can be paid for points recovered rather than for presence
A regulator and supervisor able to enforce loss targets during the term, not only at expiry
Political tolerance for disconnecting non-paying users and prosecuting theft, which is where non-technical losses are recovered
pattern.travelled: Loss-reduction management contracts are a common utility reform. This case shows the first two years of gains disappearing once enforcement weakened, and a government that ended up reabsorbing the function it had contracted out.

records.title: Aeropuerto Internacional de Palmerola
records.claim: Honduras's Infrastructure Secretariat concessioned the Palmerola international airport to Palmerola International Airport S.A., with a USD 87.1 million reference investment. Works began on 5 December 2016 and operations on 11 December 2021, about 60 months after works began, against a 61-month contracted works period (start of operation is not necessarily completion of works).

metric.name: Months from start of works (2016-12-05) to start of operation (2021-12-11), computed

secondMetric.name: Contracted works execution period

source.publisher: Superintendencia de Alianza Público Privada (SAPP), Honduras, Palmerola concession fact sheet

records.limits: The schedule figure is ours, computed from two dates on the regulator's fact sheet: about 60 months against a 61-month contracted period. The sheet does not say whether the works period was amended, extended or suspended, or whether 'start of operation' means full completion. The only cost figure is a reference investment set at signature. No final cost, cost overrun or state contribution is published there, so this record shows schedule performance only and is silent on cost, which is half of what the indicator asks. The terminal was built at an existing air base with a runway, which makes it an easier build than a greenfield airport. SAPP is the concession's own regulator. Other SAPP sheets carry copy errors (the EEH sheet cites airport revenues), so treat field values with care. Passenger demand, the concession's financial health and whether the airport displaced Toncontín as intended are not shown.

pattern.mechanism: Honduras's Infrastructure Secretariat let a 34-and-a-half-year concession with a fixed works period, had Congress approve it and a trust carry it, and left SAPP and a supervising consortium to hold the concessionaire to the schedule.
preconditions: A PPP law and a regulator able to publish and enforce contract milestones
An existing site and runway that removed most land acquisition and airside risk
Private bank financing that reached financial close (August 2018) before the main works

records.title: Instituto Técnico de Capacitación y Productividad (INTECAP)
records.claim: Guatemala's employer-levy-funded training institute INTECAP reported 490,280 participants in 26,387 vocational training events in 2025, 99.72% of its operating-plan target, through centres in all 22 departments.

metric.name: Participants in vocational training events (total formación profesional)

secondMetric.name: Vocational training events delivered

source.publisher: Instituto Técnico de Capacitación y Productividad (INTECAP), Resultados Finales de Estadísticas Operativas 2025 (G.E.DP-01)

records.limits: This is INTECAP reporting on itself against its own operating plan. Nobody audits the count. Participants are enrolments in events, not unique people: one worker who takes three courses counts three times, so the figure cannot be divided by the adult population to give a participation rate, which is what the indicator asks for. Most of the volume is short: seminars (202,359) and the ACTA line (218,147) make up about 86% of participants, while the long technical careers (CTO, CTM, CTMS) total about 13,400. Some programmes, such as FORJA and the mid-level technical careers, enrol young people, so not every participant is an adult learner. The text layer garbles the event columns of several national rows, though the total row reads cleanly. The figure covers one year only. No series is given here, so this record cannot say whether participation is rising or falling, and it says nothing about completion, certification or labour-market outcomes.

pattern.mechanism: Guatemala's Congress gave a joint state-employer institute a compulsory 1% payroll levy, collected by the social security institute, and the institute turned it into a national network of training centres and short courses for workers at every occupational level.
preconditions: A formal payroll base large enough to fund training through a levy collected alongside social security contributions
Employer representation in governance, so firms accept the levy as their own training budget
Centres in every department, which reach formal workers and leave the large informal workforce mostly outside
pattern.travelled: It follows the Latin American levy-funded training model (SENAI, SENA, INA), and like them it reaches the formal sector far better than informal workers.

records.title: INSAFORP tripartite training institute, and its dissolution
records.claim: El Salvador ran its national vocational training system from 1993 through INSAFORP, an institute funded by a 1% employer payroll levy and governed by a tripartite council of four government, four employer and four worker representatives; a 2021 reform gave the President the choice of the employer seats, and Decree 893 of 14 November 2023 dissolved INSAFORP and handed its functions to INCAF, whose council holds only the institute's president and four ministries.

metric.name: Employer-sector seats on the governing council of the national training institute under the 2023 INCAF law

secondMetric.name: Employer-sector seats on the INSAFORP Consejo Directivo under the 1993 Ley de Formación Profesional (peak structure, as read from the recital of the 2021 reform)

source.publisher: Legislative Assembly of El Salvador, Decreto N.° 893 (Ley del Instituto Nacional de Capacitación y Formación), as published by the Supreme Court's Centro de Documentación Judicial

records.limits: The metric is a count of seats read off the text of two laws, not a measured outcome: the value 0 is our reading of Art. 11 of Decree 893, which lists only the INCAF president and four ministries, and the peak of four employer seats comes from a recital in the 2021 reform, not from the 1993 law itself, which we did not open. The 1% levy rate in the claim is read from Art. 19 of Decree 893, which carries the levy over, and was not read from the 1993 text. Neither text shows how much the employer and worker seats shaped training decisions in practice, how many people INSAFORP trained, or whether training volume or quality fell under INCAF; no official participant series was retrieved, so this record documents the end of a governance arrangement, not a fall in delivery. Firms still fund the system: Art. 19 keeps the 1% employer payroll levy, although it reserves only 20% of it for INCAF's training and sends the remaining 80% elsewhere, so the levy-funded collaboration was reshaped rather than abolished in money terms. The collaboration was already eroded before dissolution: the 2021 reform let the President pick employer representatives from ternas built by the Labour Ministry, without requiring membership of employer associations. The Supreme Court documentation host returned intermittent HTTP 522 errors on the day of retrieval before serving both documents.

pattern.mechanism: El Salvador's Legislative Assembly, on the executive's initiative, first moved the choice of INSAFORP's employer representatives to the President (2021) and then dissolved the tripartite institute, replacing it with a ministry-run council while keeping the employer payroll levy (2023). The state kept the money flow from firms and removed the firms' and workers' seats at the table.
preconditions: A training system financed by an employer payroll levy, so the state can keep the revenue while changing who governs it
A legislative majority aligned with the executive, able to pass an institutional replacement in a single session
Employer and worker organisations whose seats rested on ordinary statute rather than on constitutional or treaty protection
pattern.travelled: Levy-funded tripartite training bodies of the SENAI and INFOTEP family exist across Latin America; the Salvadoran case shows the arrangement is only as durable as the statute that seats the private sector, since the levy alone does not guarantee a voice.

records.title: El Chaparral (3 de Febrero) hydroelectric plant
records.claim: El Salvador's state hydro commission CEL financed the El Chaparral hydroelectric plant on the Torola River through a BCIE loan arranged in September 2008, with four planned years of construction, and inaugurated it as the 3 de Febrero plant on 19 October 2023 at an approximate cost of US$800 million; CEL gives the initial investment as US$207.8 million, so the final cost is about 3.8 times the initial figure, some 15 years after the 2008 loan.

metric.name: Approximate final cost of the 3 de Febrero (El Chaparral) hydroelectric plant, stated at inauguration

secondMetric.name: Initial investment of the El Chaparral project, as stated by CEL in 2022

source.publisher: Comisión Ejecutiva Hidroeléctrica del Río Lempa (CEL), inauguration notice for the 3 de Febrero hydroelectric plant

records.limits: Both cost figures come from the executing agency reporting on its own project, and both are stated loosely: the final figure is the President's "costo aproximado" quoted in a CEL news item, not an audited account, and CEL's own 2022 notice gave the final cost as "more than $750 million" while the President's speech gave the initial cost as $200 million rather than $207.8 million. The overrun ratio of about 3.8 is our computation from two different documents, and CEL gives the initial figure with no year: it appears to be the price for a design later replaced after technical failures, so part of the gap reflects a changed scope, not only cost escalation; no figure separates the two. The cost statements are politically framed, attributing the overrun to previous governments, and the government that completed the plant is the source. No Court of Accounts final audit was retrieved. The start year rests on the date of the first BCIE loan reported by the Assembly, not on a published construction start date, and the 15-year span is computed from that date to inauguration; the four-year planned duration comes only from the President's quoted speech. The figures say nothing about the plant's output, which is 65.8 MW of installed capacity per the Assembly page.

pattern.mechanism: CEL contracted a 65.8 MW dam, financed by BCIE loans the Assembly guaranteed, and when the original design failed it refinanced a redesign through two further BCIE loans and completed the plant under a later government. Successive administrations kept financing the asset rather than abandoning it, at the price of a cost multiple.
preconditions: A state utility with borrowing capacity and access to a regional development bank willing to extend and enlarge loans
Geological and design studies whose adequacy is only tested once excavation begins
A legislature that keeps guaranteeing sovereign debt for a stalled project across changes of government
pattern.travelled: The case sits with other hydro and power projects in the corpus whose initial prices did not hold; it shows that an initial contract price transfers little risk when the state must pay for a redesign to finish the asset.

records.title: INFOTEP national technical and vocational training
records.claim: The Dominican Republic's tripartite training institute INFOTEP, created by Law 116-80 in 1980, registered 1,027,791 participants in training actions nationwide in 2025 and 3,613,098 participants between August 2020 and August 2025.

metric.name: Participants in INFOTEP training actions nationwide

secondMetric.name: Participants trained by INFOTEP, August 2020 to August 2025

source.publisher: Presidency of the Dominican Republic, reporting INFOTEP's Memoria Institucional 2025

records.limits: The figures are INFOTEP's own administrative counts, relayed by the presidency's news service from the institute's annual report; the report itself was not opened, because infotep.gob.do refused scripted requests (HTTP 403). A participant is an enrolment in a training action, not a person: someone taking several short courses counts several times, so the number cannot be read as a share of adults trained and is not comparable with survey participation rates. The two figures are hard to reconcile: 3.6 million over five years averages about 720,000 a year, against more than one million in 2025 alone, and nothing on the pages explains the jump, whether a definition changed, or how much of it is short or virtual courses. The counts include young people who may not be adults in the survey sense, and they say nothing about course length, completion, certification rates, or labour-market outcomes. The pages are promotional and were published by the government that runs the institute.

pattern.mechanism: The Dominican state, employers and unions run INFOTEP jointly under Law 116-80, financed by an employer payroll contribution, and since 2020 the institute expanded its own centres and virtual offer to push enrolment past one million a year.
preconditions: A compulsory employer training levy that gives the institute a revenue base independent of the annual budget contest
Tripartite governance that keeps employers invested in the course offer
A dense network of own and partner training centres, plus a virtual platform, to reach provinces outside Santo Domingo
pattern.travelled: INFOTEP belongs to the Latin American levy-funded training family with SENAI and SENA; El Salvador dissolved its counterpart, INSAFORP, in 2023, so the same model travelled and was then unwound next door.

records.title: Programa Ampliado de Inmunizaciones, and its erosion
records.claim: WHO and UNICEF estimated Venezuela's national DTP3 coverage among one-year-olds at 50 percent in 2025, down from 87 percent in 2015, and coverage has not returned above 66 percent in any year since 2017.

metric.name: Estimated DTP3 coverage among 1-year-olds

secondMetric.name: Estimated DTP3 coverage at the 2015 peak

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Global Health Observatory: DTP3 immunization coverage among 1-year-olds (WUENIC)

records.limits: Construct fit is borrowed, not literal: DTP3 coverage is not the cost or schedule performance of an infrastructure project. It is filed here only on the bra-pni precedent, which EVIDENCE.md names as the reversal template (hti-immunization-erosion files the same kind of series under disaster_preparedness instead); a reviewer holding to the literal construct should reject it. The 87 percent peak is a single good year in a volatile series (50 in 2008, 87 in 2005 and 2015), and the WHO/UNICEF 2022-revision country profile (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/country-profiles/immunization/2023-country-profiles/immunization_ven_2023.pdf) says the 2015 rise was 'due in part to a change in the population source', so part of the drop is a denominator artefact. Estimates rest on Venezuelan administrative reports with no nationally representative survey in the last five years; WHO/UNICEF graded recent years as having no accepted empirical data, and values are revised between rounds (2022 was 56 in the 2022 revision and 43 now). The same profile records national vaccine and syringe stockouts from 2016 to 2020, which locates the failure in supply rather than in the programme's design, but the series cannot separate economic collapse, emigration of health workers, sanctions-era procurement limits and denominator error. DTP3 is one antigen. PAHO separately documented that endemic measles transmission was re-established in Venezuela in 2018 and interrupted again in 2019 (https://journal.paho.org/en/articles/comprehensive-approach-achieving-reverification-measles-elimination-venezuela-2019-2023), which supports the erosion but is not part of this metric.

pattern.mechanism: Venezuela's health ministry ran a free national schedule through public clinics and held DTP3 near or above 80 percent for most of 2009 to 2016; when national procurement of vaccines and syringes failed during the economic collapse, the ministry kept the programme formally in place while coverage fell to around half of infants.
preconditions: Hard-currency budgets and procurement able to keep vaccines and syringes in national stock
A clinic network staffed by vaccinators who stay through a crisis
Population denominators accurate enough that a fall in coverage is seen before an outbreak reveals it
pattern.travelled: Haiti shows the same erosion from stockouts and weak reporting; Venezuela adds that a fall can sit inside a denominator change for two years before an outbreak (measles in 2017 to 2019) makes it visible.

records.title: SINAPRED evacuation for hurricanes Eta and Iota
records.claim: Nicaragua's national disaster system, SINAPRED, evacuated 160,597 people and sheltered 59,964 ahead of hurricanes Eta and Iota in November 2020, when about 3 million people were exposed, and 21 lives were reported lost.

metric.name: People evacuated in Nicaragua for hurricanes Eta and Iota

secondMetric.name: Lives lost in Nicaragua to hurricanes Eta and Iota

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Information Document, Nicaragua Hurricanes Eta and Iota Emergency Response Project (P175878), report PIDA31028

records.limits: The World Bank document is an appraisal-stage project information note written days after landfall (dated 23 November 2020), and its evacuation, shelter and death figures are the Nicaraguan government's own preliminary counts relayed by the Bank, not an independent verification; the Nicaraguan government's casualty reporting has been disputed in other emergencies, notably COVID-19. The figures show people moved and lives reported lost, not how many people at risk were not reached, the conditions in shelters during a pandemic, or the speed and quality of recovery: the same document puts damage and losses at USD 738.6 million, about 6.2 percent of GDP. Low deaths also depend on where the storms struck (the sparsely populated North Caribbean Coast) and on forecast lead time from regional meteorological centres, so the count is not a clean measure of SINAPRED alone. The 1994-2013 average of 160 hydrometeorological deaths a year is a different set of hazards and is context, not a counterfactual. SINAPRED's own site did not open from here (connection timeout), so the government primary source could not be checked. One hurricane season is a single test.

pattern.mechanism: Nicaragua's government built a statutory disaster system under Law 337 that runs a national operations committee and a technical arm (INETER), and used it in 2020 to move about 160,000 people out of the path of two major hurricanes within two weeks.
preconditions: A statutory chain of command from national committee to municipal and community brigades
Forecasting and early warning that give days of lead time before landfall
A centralised state able to order and enforce evacuation, which in Nicaragua's case comes with weak independent oversight of its reported results
pattern.travelled: The same sequence of statutory system, community brigades and pre-landfall evacuation underlies Cuba's hurricane record; where the state is less centralised, the evacuation step depends more on trust in warnings than on command.

records.title: National cholera elimination drive, and the return of cholera
records.claim: After Haiti's Ministry of Public Health (MSPP) and water directorate DINEPA launched the National Plan for the Elimination of Cholera in 2013, the country reported no confirmed cholera case from January 2019 to January 2022, but transmission returned in October 2022 and the MSPP epidemiology directorate had reported 76,675 suspected cases in all 10 departments by 18 December 2023.

metric.name: Suspected cholera cases reported since the October 2022 re-emergence

secondMetric.name: Consecutive years with no confirmed cholera case before re-emergence

source.publisher: Pan American Health Organization / WHO, Cholera Epidemic in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, Situation Report #20 (27 December 2023), citing MSPP/DELR

records.limits: The two numbers are in different units: a three-year run with zero confirmed cases is set against a cumulative count of suspected cases, so the record shows a loss of the elimination outcome, not a measured fall in a capability. Part of the apparent elimination may be under-detection; WHO reports national figures and does not audit them. Suspected-case counts depend on clinical definitions and reporting under gang violence that cut access to clinics and labs, so the 76,675 figure is likely an undercount and not comparable with the 2010 to 2019 series. The re-emergence was driven mainly by insecurity, displacement and the collapse of water supply, which the elimination plan's water and sanitation targets never fixed; it is weak evidence about the surveillance and rapid-response capacity itself. Much of the response (rapid response teams, oral vaccine, water investments) was financed and technically run with PAHO, UNICEF, CDC and NGOs, so attribution to Haitian institutions alone is partial. The started year, 2013, is the year the plan was announced and funding requested, since the PAHO page is a funding call, and not a dated start of delivery; control activities had run since the October 2010 outbreak. The secondMetric comes from a separate WHO page.

pattern.mechanism: Haiti's MSPP and DINEPA pursued elimination through case surveillance, case-area rapid response teams and targeted vaccination, with partner financing, and drove confirmed transmission to zero. When insecurity, displacement and water-system collapse returned in 2022, the response chain broke and cholera spread back to every department.
preconditions: Laboratory-confirmed surveillance with field teams able to reach every reported case within days
Safe water and sanitation coverage that removes the transmission route, not only emergency treatment
Enough security and sustained financing to keep response teams and supplies moving after donor attention fades
pattern.travelled: Case-area targeted response has been copied in other cholera-endemic settings, and Haiti shows it can push transmission to zero without fixing the water system, which leaves the result reversible.

records.title: PetroCaribe-financed public investment programme, and its audited failure
records.claim: From September 2008 to September 2016, Haiti's Council of Ministers allocated PetroCaribe oil-credit revenue to 409 public projects, and the state fuel monetisation bureau BMPAD disbursed US$1,605,905,287.84 (92.4% of the revised budget), but the Superior Court of Auditors (CSCCA) found cost and schedule overruns across the audited works, including a Cap-Haïtien street rehabilitation that ran 18% over budget and took 21 months against an eight-month contract term.

metric.name: PetroCaribe project funds disbursed by BMPAD across 409 Council-of-Ministers projects
metric.unit: US dollars (cumulative, 92.4% of revised budget of US$1,738,691,909.70)

secondMetric.name: Budget overrun on the audited Cap-Haïtien street rehabilitation, phase 1 (MTPTC)

source.publisher: Cour Supérieure des Comptes et du Contentieux Administratif (CSCCA), Audit spécifique de gestion du fonds PetroCaribe, rapport 3 (August 2020)

records.limits: The headline number is money disbursed, not works delivered: the CSCCA itself says missing reception certificates often stop it concluding whether a contract was finished or abandoned, and it documents abandoned works such as the Miragoâne market and bus station, stopped at 35.27% progress, a figure from report 1 (31 January 2019). The court publishes no aggregate cost or schedule overrun for the 409 projects. The 18% overrun is one audited road project picked as the cost figure, with no claim that it is typical; other audited projects show overruns of 9%, 10%, 33% and 54% against contract (reports 1 and 3), and some came in under budget.
