Real-terms cuts to the adult budget and the move of level 3 and above provision onto learner loans roughly halved adult participation within a decade.
preconditions: A national network of further education colleges and adult community learning services funded by central government
A learner-level administrative record that every funded provider must return
A funding settlement that can be cut without legislation, which is what made the erosion possible

records.title: Educación Básica Alternativa (EBA), and its erosion
records.claim: Peru's Educación Básica Alternativa, the second-chance basic education modality for youths and adults, enrolled 226,500 students in 2016, the highest year of the 2014 to 2023 table, and 190,700 in 2023, according to INEI's Compendio Estadístico 2024 citing the Ministry of Education's school census.

metric.name: Enrolment in Educación Básica Alternativa

secondMetric.name: Enrolment in Educación Básica Alternativa at the 2016 peak of the 2014 to 2023 series

source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática (INEI), Perú: Compendio Estadístico 2024, Tomo 1, Table 5.6 (source: Ministerio de Educación, Censo Escolar, Unidad de Estadística Educativa)

records.limits: The numbers are in a PDF table (Table 5.6, PDF page 323 of 1,046), published in thousands with one decimal, and INEI republishes the Ministry of Education's census rather than collecting it; the Ministry's own ESCALE portal sits behind a bot-verification wall and could not be read. The peak is only the highest year of the ten-year window the table shows (2014 to 2023), and it was a one-year jump: enrolment was 204,500 in 2014 and 203,900 in 2015, so against 2014 the 2023 count is only about 7 percent lower, and the fall of about 16 percent is measured from that jump. The series reached its low of 188,600 in 2022 and rose slightly in 2023. The modality serves adolescents from 14 as well as adults, so not every learner is an adult, and the table does not split public from private centres. Enrolment is a census-day count, not attendance or completion, and a smaller EBA can partly reflect more young people completing regular schooling. A table footnote says the conversion of former adult education centres into the modality has been under way since 2006, so early years mix old and new structures. The 2003 start is the Ley General de Educación 28044 that created the modality, which is not stated at the source URL.

pattern.mechanism: The 2003 General Education Law converted Peru's old adult schools into a separate modality of basic education, delivered by public and private CEBA centres with flexible schedules and counted in the national school census. Enrolment peaked in 2016 and has drifted down since.
preconditions: A school census run by the education ministry that reports enrolment by modality
An existing network of adult and evening schools that could be converted rather than built
A legal definition that lets learners certify primary and secondary completion outside the regular track

records.title: Upper secondary education for adults in non-stationary study
records.claim: Estonia's secondary schools for adults and the non-stationary departments of other schools enrolled 7,866 learners in upper secondary education in 2025, the highest number in the Statistics Estonia series that starts in 1990, while the number of dedicated adult secondary schools fell from 16 in 2016 to nine.

metric.name: Enrolments in upper secondary education in non-stationary general education

secondMetric.name: Secondary schools for adults

source.publisher: Statistics Estonia, table HT234: Enrolments, graduates and schools in non-stationary general education

records.limits: The scale is small: 7,866 enrolments in a country of about 1.4 million people, and non-stationary general education is only one part of adult learning, leaving out vocational schools, universities, employer training and the unemployment fund's courses. Enrolment rose from 5,653 in 2022 to 7,866 in 2025, and the source does not say why; part of the rise may come from refugees from Ukraine and from young people who left day school, so the count is not purely adults returning to study. Basic education enrolments in the same table fell from a 2005 high of 1,722 to 588 in 2025, so the record is not a story of growth across the board. Fewer dedicated adult schools (16 in 2016, nine in 2025) means provision was consolidated, and more schools now teach adults through non-stationary departments (27 in 2025). The 1990 start is the first year of the published series, not the start of adult schooling in Estonia, and the table's reference year should be read as the school year beginning that autumn.

pattern.mechanism: The state and municipalities keep a network of adult gymnasiums and let ordinary schools run evening, distance and part-time departments that teach the national upper secondary curriculum free of charge to adults. When the network shrank, enrolment moved into consolidated schools and departments rather than disappearing.
preconditions: A national curriculum and state examinations that are the same for adult and day learners
School funding that follows a learner into non-stationary study
A small, digitally administered school system in which consolidating adult schools did not cut access

records.title: Department of Skill Development skill-upgrading training
records.claim: Thailand's Department of Skill Development, through 86 national institutes and provincial offices, trained 91,911 workers in skill-upgrading courses in fiscal year 2023, of whom 88,656 completed, according to its open-data release.

metric.name: Workers completing skill-upgrading training (sum of male and female completers across all units)

secondMetric.name: Workers completing skill-upgrading training in fiscal year 2564

source.publisher: Department of Skill Development, Ministry of Labour, open data portal, dataset dsd_12_01_01 'Number of workers completing skill-upgrading training' (CSV per fiscal year)

records.limits: Both numbers are computed: the department publishes one row per unit and occupation group (494 rows in fiscal 2566), and the totals here are the sums of its male and female completer columns, which the department does not print as a headline. The CSV is encoded in Thai Windows code page 874, and some cells carry a thousands separator, so a sum that parses them as text undercounts. The open data stops at fiscal 2566 (2023) and covers three years only (88,602 completers in fiscal 2564, 63,785 in fiscal 2565, 88,656 in fiscal 2566), so no long trend or peak can be read from it. About 89,000 completers a year is roughly 0.2 percent of a labour force near 40 million, the courses are short, and the count is the agency reporting on itself with no outcome measure. The figures cover the department's own upgrading courses only, not pre-employment training, supplementary occupation courses, employer training claimed under the Skill Development Promotion Act, or the education ministry's non-formal education, whose portals refused connections from this research. The 1993 start date is the founding of the department as given in general references, not stated at the source URL.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Labour runs a national network of skill development institutes and provincial offices that deliver short, free upgrading courses to employed workers by occupation group, and publishes per-unit results as open data.
preconditions: A labour ministry department with its own training centres in every region
Occupational skill standards that courses can be built against
An open-data mandate that makes each unit report applicants, entrants and completers

records.title: Adult literacy education under the National Commission for Mass Literacy, Adult and Non-Formal Education
records.claim: Enrolment in adult literacy education in Nigeria, reported by the National Commission for Mass Literacy, Adult and Non-Formal Education, rose from 322,288 in 2020 to 2,152,146 in 2021 and 2,915,453 in 2022, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

metric.name: Total enrolment in adult literacy education

secondMetric.name: Total enrolment in adult literacy education in 2020

source.publisher: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Social Statistics Report 2023 (published March 2024), section 1.1.1 and Figure 1.1 (source: National Commission for Mass Literacy, Adult and Non-Formal Education)

records.limits: The figure is an administrative count supplied by the commission to the statistics office, which republishes it without a definition: it does not say whether enrolment counts people or registrations, whether state-run and donor-funded centres are included, or how many learners completed. A ninefold rise in two years is not explained in the report; 2020 was depressed by pandemic closures, and the jump may also reflect better reporting coverage rather than more learning. The series covers three years only, so no peak or trend before 2020 can be read. The number is in a PDF (Figure 1.1 and its text, PDF page 10), and the newest year is 2022. Even 2.9 million enrolments is small against the large non-literate adult population the commission targets, and literacy classes are basic education, not the training-for-work participation most adult-learning surveys count. The 1990 start is the decree that established the commission, not stated at the source URL.

pattern.mechanism: A federal commission sets adult literacy and non-formal education policy and funds and coordinates state agencies for mass education that run community literacy centres with volunteer and paid facilitators, reporting enrolment upward to the national statistics office.
preconditions: State agencies for mass education in every state to run the centres
Facilitators paid little or nothing, which keeps the count high and the quality uncertain
An administrative reporting line from centres to the federal commission and on to the statistics office

records.title: Skills Development under the Labour Market Development Agreements, and its 2024-25 funding cut
records.claim: Canada's provinces and territories delivered 154,892 employment-benefit services under the federally funded Labour Market Development Agreements in 2024-25, 92 percent of them Skills Development training, in a year when Part II funding fell by $425 million as a temporary top-up in place since 2016-17 ended and Skills Development spending fell 19.7 percent to $798.9 million.

metric.name: Employment Benefits services delivered under the LMDAs (92 percent Skills Development)

secondMetric.name: Expenditure on Skills Development under the LMDAs, down 19.7 percent from 2023-24

source.publisher: Employment and Social Development Canada for the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, Employment Insurance Monitoring and Assessment Report 2024-25, Chapter 3

records.limits: The counts are services (interventions), not people: one client can hold several, and the department reports 502,007 clients across all LMDA services, most of them in employment assistance rather than training. The erosion rests on money, not on a measured fall in training: the chapter's introduction says Part II received $425 million less in 2024-25 because the temporary additional funding in place since 2016-17 sunset, and Skills Development spending fell 19.7 percent. Employment Benefits services also fell, from 192,365 in 2023-24 (Table 3.1.2.3) to 154,892, but nearly all of that is Skills Development Regular falling 37.8 percent to 62,084, which the table note attributes to a coding correction that moved provincial workshops out of that category; the services fall is therefore not counted as the loss here, and apprenticeship services rose 3.2 percent to 80,376. 2023-24 is the previous year, not a demonstrated all-time peak. The programme reports on itself, and the 92 percent share is stated by the department (62,084 plus 80,376 of 154,892). The started year is the date the first bilateral agreements were signed (Alberta and New Brunswick, December 1996, per the LMDA page on canada.ca), not stated in this chapter. The training is for EI-eligible workers, a subset of all adults, and the record says nothing about outcomes.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government channels Employment Insurance Part II money to provinces and territories through bilateral agreements, and each province buys or delivers skills training and apprenticeship support for EI-eligible workers, reporting to a common monitoring framework.
preconditions: A contributory unemployment insurance fund large enough to finance active measures
Provincial employment services able to deliver training under federal money
An annual monitoring report that counts interventions the same way across 13 jurisdictions
pattern.travelled: Temporary federal top-ups raised volumes for eight years; when the top-up sunset the training budget fell with it, which is the usual fate of active measures financed as supplements rather than baseline.

records.title: Instituto Nacional de Formación Profesional (INFOP)
records.claim: Honduras's national vocational training institute INFOP trained or certified 326,161 people in 2024 across six programmes and about 12,552 courses, figures the Tribunal Superior de Cuentas checked against instructors' start and end reports.

metric.name: People trained or certified by INFOP across its six programmes (sum of six programme totals)

secondMetric.name: People certified in the largest programme, Tourism, Commerce and Services

source.publisher: Tribunal Superior de Cuentas de Honduras, Informe RC-Nº32-2025-DVGP-INFOP, evaluation of INFOP's 2024 accountability report

records.limits: The total is computed by us: the audit report (pages 9 to 10 of the PDF) gives six programme results, 24,181 (agriculture), 15,834 (industrial), 135,430 (tourism, commerce and services), 65,035 (ICT), 84,665 (company agreements) and 1,016 (labour competency certification), and no single total; the press figure of 325,145 is the first five. The counts are participations per programme product, not unique adults, so a person who took two courses counts twice. Many courses are short, about 20 hours at the low end, and the list includes soft-skills topics such as customer service and motivation; the industrial programme serves ages 15 to 25, so part of the count is youth. The numbers originate in INFOP's own reports; the Tribunal verified them against signed instructor reports and a sample of 68 participants per product, not by a full audit. Over-execution of up to 165 percent against plan says the targets were low, not that demand was met. The 2021 evaluation records that INFOP cancelled its programme for vulnerable groups after the pandemic, so coverage of the poorest is not shown here. The started year is the 1972 decree law creating INFOP, stated in the report.

pattern.mechanism: A levy-funded autonomous training institute, financed by employer and worker contributions, runs its own centres and contracts courses through business chambers and unions, and the supreme audit institution checks its delivery figures each year.
preconditions: A payroll levy that gives the institute its own revenue
Business chambers and unions willing to host company-agreement courses
An audit office that reviews physical delivery, not only spending
pattern.travelled: The levy-funded national training institute is the Latin American model (SENA, INA, INTECAP, INFOTEP); Honduras's version leans heavily on short courses and outsourced company training.

records.title: Ministry of Labour Vocational Training Division adult courses
records.claim: Israel's Vocational Training Division, in the labour ministry, trained about 61,000 people in 2022, against about 55,000 in 2019 and 59,000 in 2021, according to the Knesset Research and Information Center.

metric.name: People trained through the Vocational Training Division

secondMetric.name: People trained through the Vocational Training Division, pre-pandemic year

source.publisher: Knesset Research and Information Center, Review of poverty data in Israel and government policy (26 September 2023), citing labour ministry data

records.limits: The figures are rounded and reach us through the Knesset's research centre, which republishes labour ministry data; the sentence is on PDF page 11 (printed page 9), in Hebrew. Most of the volume is not state-funded training: the Center's December 2021 paper on the training system says that in 2019, 49,192 of the participants, 88.5 percent, were in non-budgeted courses that learners pay for at private institutions the Division supervises and certifies, and 5,621 were in state-funded courses. The same paper records a fall to 36,522 participants in 2020, which the ministry attributed to the absence of a state budget and the pandemic; the 2022 figure shows recovery, so the record is not filed as a reversal. About 61,000 a year is a small share of Israel's adult population, and the count says nothing about completion or employment outcomes. The started year is not given in either source: 2003 is the year a 2006 European Training Foundation report gives for the Division's predecessor bureau moving to the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Labour, and the bureau ran adult courses before that.

pattern.mechanism: The labour ministry's training division licenses and supervises a large market of paid vocational courses, sets curricula and state certification exams for more than 350 occupations, and funds a smaller set of courses through referrals from the employment service.
preconditions: State certification exams that employers recognise
Private and franchised training centres that can be supervised
A referral channel from the employment service for funded places
pattern.travelled: The supervised paid-course model keeps volume up when budgets fail, as in 2020, but it also means the state-funded core is a small fraction of the headline count.

records.title: Educación Permanente para personas jóvenes y adultas (MEC)
records.claim: Paraguay's Ministry of Education and Sciences enrolled 94,436 young people and adults in its four formal and non-formal Educación Permanente programmes in 2025, as reported in the Ministry of Economy and Finance's budget evaluation for that year.

metric.name: Students enrolled in the four formal and non-formal Educación Permanente programmes for young people and adults

source.publisher: Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas del Paraguay, Informe Financiero 2025, Tomo II: Control Financiero y Evaluación Presupuestaria (MEC section)

records.limits: The number sits in one sentence on printed page 34 (PDF page 35) of a budget evaluation, sourced in its footnote to the education ministry's own reporting (SIME N° 5.130/2026); the ministry is reporting on itself through the finance ministry. The programmes serve people aged 15 and over, so part of the count is youth rather than adults, and enrolment is not completion. 94,436 is about 2 percent of Paraguay's adult population, so this evidences a standing national second-chance system, not broad adult participation. The four programmes are not broken out, and no earlier year is given on this page, so no trend can be read; the education ministry's open-data portal, which carries the enrolment series, did not respond from here. The started year is the 1998 General Education Law that set out permanent education for young people and adults; it is not stated in the source.

pattern.mechanism: The education ministry runs basic, secondary and vocational second-chance programmes for over-age learners through a national network of centres, many hosted in ordinary schools in the evening, and reports enrolment through the budget-by-results system.
preconditions: Schools that can host evening classes for adults
A ministry directorate dedicated to youth and adult education
A budget reporting system that asks for physical results, not only spending

records.title: National literacy campaigns, 2010-2015
records.claim: Haiti's national literacy campaigns trained about 250,000 adults between 2010 and 2015, about 10 percent of the illiterate population, according to the education ministry's ten-year plan.

metric.name: Adults trained in literacy campaigns

source.publisher: Ministère de l'Éducation Nationale et de la Formation Professionnelle (MENFP), Plan décennal d'éducation et de formation 2020-2030 (December 2020), republished by the MIT-Haiti Initiative

records.limits: The only figure is a rounded approximation on printed page 25 (PDF page 28) of the ministry's plan, which cites an unpublished 2017 MENFP review of the 2010-2015 operational plan; no annual series, completion or literacy test results are given. 'Trained' is not 'made literate'. The copy that opens is hosted by the MIT-Haiti Initiative, not by the ministry, whose own site does not carry the PDF. The plan places the adult literacy campaigns, itinerant courses of at most six months, under a Secretariat of State (the Secrétairerie d'État à l'Alphabétisation; printed page 21, PDF page 24), but it does not say who paid for them; Haiti's literacy work in this period drew on foreign cooperation, so the domestic share of the funding is unknown. The same page says non-formal education suffers from inadequate infrastructure, budgets and staff, and the record does not show the campaigns continuing after 2015. 2010 is the start of the reporting period, not the start of literacy campaigns in Haiti.

pattern.mechanism: The state ran adult literacy campaigns through the education ministry's literacy apparatus, reaching an estimated tenth of the illiterate adult population over five years.
preconditions: Volunteer or low-cost literacy facilitators
Foreign cooperation to fund materials and training
Enough stability for community classes to meet

records.title: Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements
records.claim: The Australian Government paid $3.1 billion to state and territory governments through the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements between 1 June 2018 and 30 June 2022, and the arrangements were activated for 49 disaster events that occurred in 2021–22.

metric.name: DRFA payments to states and territories

secondMetric.name: Disaster events that occurred in 2021–22 with DRFA activations

source.publisher: Australian National Audit Office, Auditor-General Report No. 23 of 2022–23, Administration of the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements

records.limits: Dollars paid measure the federal share of state recovery spending, which tracks how much damage the hazards did as much as how well recovery was run: a bad flood year raises the number. The audit is an independent assurance review of administration, not an evaluation of recovery outcomes, and it found the agencies did not monitor or report DRFA performance, so no figure on speed or quality of recovery exists to set beside the spending. The 49 events is the ANAO's own headline count of disasters that occurred in 2021–22 and activated the arrangements; it counts activations, not their size or how well each was handled. Delivery is by the states; the Commonwealth reimburses. The ANAO site sits behind a Cloudflare check that blocks scripted requests, and its headline counter renders as 0 without JavaScript; the numbers were read in a browser at the same URL, and 49 also appears in paragraph 2.16. DRFA replaced the earlier Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements in 2018, so the start year is that of the current determination, not of federal recovery cost sharing.

pattern.mechanism: The Commonwealth pre-commits by ministerial determination to reimburse a set share of state and territory relief and recovery spending in defined categories once an event is activated, so states can spend first and claim afterwards under an agreed assurance process.
preconditions: A federal fiscal capacity large enough to absorb a bad disaster year
State governments able to design, run and acquit relief programmes
An assurance process both levels of government accept, which the audit found still lacked performance monitoring
pattern.travelled: Canada's DFAA is the older version of the same cost-sharing move. Both reached modernisation reviews that pushed toward funding mitigation, because a reimbursement scheme alone pays to rebuild what the next event can destroy again.

records.title: Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements
records.claim: Public Safety Canada's Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements paid $1.84 billion in contributions to provinces and territories between 2011–12 and 2015–16, almost 45 percent of everything paid since the programme began in 1970, while 53 disaster events were approved by the Governor in Council between 2011 and 2016.

metric.name: DFAA contributions paid

secondMetric.name: Disaster events approved by the Governor in Council

source.publisher: Public Safety Canada, 2016–2017 Evaluation of the Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements (final report, 2017-03-14)

records.limits: This is the department evaluating its own programme. Payments follow disaster losses, so a high figure is partly a record of bad luck: the 2013–14 year alone (about $1.02 billion) carries more than half the five-year total. The same evaluation shows the money arrives slowly: for the 53 events approved in 2011–2016 the estimated federal share was $3.8 billion against $1.6 billion actually issued, because provinces have up to five years after approval to request final payment, and before 2008 there was no time limit at all. The figures are nine years old; a 2025 parliamentary briefing note on the Public Safety site puts the cumulative total since 1970 at $8.9 billion, and the programme was redesigned from April 2025, so this record documents the arrangement as it stood in the evaluation period. Provinces and territories design and run the assistance; DFAA reimburses part of it.

pattern.mechanism: Ottawa cost-shares provincial and territorial response and recovery spending on a sliding scale above a per-capita threshold, triggered by an order in council, so that a single large disaster does not fall on one province's budget.
preconditions: Provinces and territories with their own disaster assistance programmes to reimburse
A federal audit and acquittal process that provinces accept, even when it takes years
Fiscal room at the federal level to absorb a spike like the 2013 Alberta floods
pattern.travelled: Australia runs the same move as the DRFA. The Canadian expert panel's 2023 report and the 2025 redesign moved money toward mitigation and earlier support for survivors, which is the usual lesson of a long-running reimbursement scheme.

records.title: National Flood Insurance Program coverage, and its erosion
records.claim: OpenFEMA's records of National Flood Insurance Program contracts in force fell from 4,667,875 on 31 December 2009 to 3,589,275 on 31 December 2025, a fall of about 23 percent in the federal flood insurance base over 16 years.

metric.name: NFIP policy contracts in force (OpenFEMA records active on the date)

secondMetric.name: NFIP policy contracts in force at the first complete year-end in the dataset

source.publisher: FEMA, OpenFEMA NFIP Redacted Policies dataset (v3)

records.limits: Both numbers are computed, not published headlines: they are the record counts the OpenFEMA API returns for policies whose effective date is on or before, and termination date after, each date, which is the method FEMA's own NFIP data FAQ gives. The 2009 figure comes from the same URL with the date changed to 2009-12-31. The count is of contracts, not policies: one condominium contract can cover many units, and FEMA's own 'NFIP by the Numbers' report for 31 August 2026 shows 3,388,273 contracts but 4,460,103 policies. The API count runs about 2 percent above FEMA's contracts-in-force report (3,589,275 against 3,512,555 for December 2025), so the level carries a small method error, though both ends use the same method. The dataset starts with policies effective in 2009, so the true earlier peak cannot be shown from it. The fall is not all lost protection: private flood insurance has grown, some properties left mapped flood zones, and Risk Rating 2.0 (2021) raised premiums by design to price risk. What the record shows is that the public programme's reach shrank, not that total insured flood exposure fell by the same amount.

pattern.mechanism: Congress created a federal insurer of last resort for flood, tied to community floodplain management and to a purchase requirement for federally backed mortgages in high-risk zones, so that recovery after floods would be paid for by premiums rather than only by disaster aid.
preconditions: Flood maps that identify who must buy and that stay current
Enforcement of the mandatory purchase requirement by lenders, which is where take-up leaks
Premiums that households will keep paying once the mortgage requirement no longer binds them
pattern.travelled: Public flood pools elsewhere (Flood Re in the United Kingdom, CCRIF for Caribbean governments, DASK for Turkish earthquakes) face the same tension: pricing risk honestly drives voluntary buyers out, and keeping them in requires subsidy or compulsion.

records.title: KMA earthquake early warning service
records.claim: The Korea Meteorological Administration expanded the national seismic network from 195 stations when its earthquake early warning service started in January 2015 to 550 stations, and by May 2026 issued early warnings within 5 to 10 seconds of first detection.

metric.name: Seismic observation stations in the national network

secondMetric.name: Seismic observation stations when the early warning service started

source.publisher: Korea Meteorological Administration, via Korea Policy Briefing (korea.kr), 15 May 2026

records.limits: This is the agency describing its own service in a government press item, in Korean. A station count is an input, and the 5 to 10 second issuance time is a stated operating standard, not a measured average over real events; the page gives no record of how warnings performed in actual earthquakes, how many were false or missed, or what share of people received the cell-broadcast text. The agency itself names the weakness: close to the epicentre, strong shaking arrives before the warning, which is why it added an on-site alert stage from 28 May 2026. Korea has had few damaging earthquakes since 2016, so the system has been tested rarely. Earlier reporting puts the 2015 issuance time at about 50 seconds, but that figure is not on this page and is not used here.

pattern.mechanism: The national weather agency densified the seismic network roughly threefold and tied automatic magnitude estimates to the national cell-broadcast emergency text system, so a warning reaches every phone in the affected area without a human approval step.
preconditions: A national cell-broadcast channel already carried by all mobile operators
Budget for a decade of station build-out and telemetry
An agency trusted to issue automatic alerts that will sometimes be wrong
pattern.travelled: Japan's JMA system is the model; Taiwan, Mexico (SASMEX) and the United States (ShakeAlert) run variants. The Korean retelling stresses network density, because a small, densely populated peninsula has little lead time between fault and city.

records.title: South African Weather Service radar network, and its erosion
records.claim: The South African Weather Service reported that the availability of its weather radar infrastructure fell from 73.83 percent in 2021/22 to 52.23 percent in 2022/23 and 44.25 percent in 2023/24, against a 75 percent target, as load shedding, missing spares and ageing C-band radars took sites down.

metric.name: Availability of RADAR infrastructure, average of quarterly performance

secondMetric.name: Availability of RADAR infrastructure

source.publisher: South African Weather Service, Annual Report 2023/24 (performance information, Programme 3), as tabled in Parliament

records.limits: The figure is in the PDF of SAWS's own annual report (printed page 70, PDF page 72), and the copy that opens is hosted by the Parliamentary Monitoring Group, a civil-society mirror of documents tabled in Parliament; the SAWS website did not serve the report to a script. 2021/22 is not shown to be the historical peak: the 2024/25 plan presented to Parliament gives 73 percent for 2020/21 as well, so the record shows a fall from a plateau, not from an all-time high. Availability is the share of time radars produced data, not forecast or warning quality, and the population covered by a working radar is not reported. The main cause named is national load shedding, an Eskom failure outside SAWS's control (see zaf-eskom-loadshedding), compounded by spares shortages and vandalism. SAWS says the ageing C-band radars will be dropped from the statistic from 2024/25, which will raise the reported figure without repairing them. The start year is SAWS's establishment under the South African Weather Service Act of 2001, which is not stated on the cited page.

pattern.mechanism: A national weather service built and ran a countrywide radar network that underpins severe-weather warnings, then let it degrade when power supply, spares contracts and maintenance budgets failed together.
preconditions: Reliable grid power or funded backup at remote radar sites
Maintenance contracts with the original manufacturer and a spares budget
Site security against theft and vandalism
pattern.travelled: The Thai warning-tower and German siren cases in this corpus show the same pattern: warning infrastructure decays quietly between disasters, because nobody measures it until it is needed.

records.title: Hunger Safety Net Programme, a shock-responsive cash transfer for drought
records.claim: Kenya's National Drought Management Authority expanded the shock-responsive Hunger Safety Net Programme from four to eight arid counties, enrolling 32,000 new households paid from the government's own budget by December 2024, while 100 percent of regular transfers in the original four counties were financed by the government.

metric.name: New regular HSNP households enrolled and paid through the government budget in expansion counties

secondMetric.name: Counties covered by the shock-responsive HSNP

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00527, Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project (P164654), 6 August 2025

records.limits: The source is the lender's completion report on a project it financed, and the numbers are in the PDF (32,000 households on printed pages 22 and 35; four to eight counties on printed page 17; drought arrears on printed page 16). The headline number is regular coverage, not drought response: the report says that during the 2021 to 2023 drought the scalable emergency component ran a deficit, emergency transfers were underfinanced and delayed, and arrears were paid only later, and that planned scale-up payments in 2024/25 were not triggered. So the record shows the standing system, not a fast drought payout. HSNP covers arid and semi-arid counties, not the whole country, by design. The 2009 start year is the first HSNP phase, which ran as a donor-funded pilot before the government took it over, and is not stated in this report.

pattern.mechanism: The drought authority pre-registers and banks almost every household in the arid north, pays the poorest a regular transfer, and uses satellite vegetation triggers to extend payments to more registered households when drought hits, so money can move without a new targeting exercise.
preconditions: A household registry and bank accounts set up before the shock
A trigger rule tied to an objective drought index
Contingent money ready to flow when the trigger fires, which is where Kenya's version fell short in 2021 to 2023
pattern.travelled: Ethiopia's PSNP and the Sahel adaptive safety nets use the same scalable design. The Kenyan retelling shows that the registry and trigger are the easy part: the contingent finance is what fails under fiscal stress.

records.title: Auxílio Reconstrução, the federal cash grant after the 2024 Rio Grande do Sul floods
records.claim: After the floods that began in late April 2024 in Rio Grande do Sul, the federal government paid R$ 2.1 billion in Auxílio Reconstrução to 429,000 families, according to the balance its extraordinary secretary for the reconstruction of Rio Grande do Sul presented to a Chamber of Deputies committee on 12 February 2025.

metric.name: Families paid the Auxílio Reconstrução

secondMetric.name: Auxílio Reconstrução paid

source.publisher: Câmara dos Deputados, Agência Câmara (hearing of the Comissão Especial sobre Prevenção e Auxílio a Desastres Naturais)

records.limits: The figure is the executive's own balance, stated by the federal secretary for the reconstruction of Rio Grande do Sul at a Chamber hearing and reported by the Chamber's news agency; it is not an audited count, and the Ministry of Integration pages that carried the running totals were behind a login wall during the 2026 electoral period, so the primary executive source could not be opened. The grant was eligibility-by-municipal-list plus self-declaration, so the count shows money reaching families, not need met: the Tribunal de Contas da União (Acórdão 1297/2025, per its news page 'Tribunal analisa benefícios a desabrigados das enchentes') found 87,300 requests (11.97%) pending for more than 100 days at 13 September 2024 and one municipality where none of 1,722 requests had been approved, and ordered the ministry to clear the backlog. The budget was sized for an estimated 375,000 families. A cash transfer is response and early recovery, not reconstruction of housing or protective works, and says nothing about whether exposure fell.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government created a flat, one-off cash grant by provisional measure within two weeks of the disaster, paid through the existing social-payment rails to families on lists the affected municipalities certified, and accepted self-declaration to trade verification for speed.
preconditions: A federal emergency-declaration process that names eligible municipalities
Payment rails and household registries that can reach families without a bank visit
Municipal civil-defence offices able to list affected households quickly
pattern.travelled: Flat post-disaster cash grants travel easily; the Brazilian case shows the bottleneck moving from paying to certifying, which is where the audit court found the delays.

records.title: Hurricane Otto priority reconstruction works
records.claim: In the 17 months to September 2018, the Instituto Costarricense de Electricidad, under an agreement with the national emergency commission (CNE), completed 64 of the 65 priority reconstruction works after Hurricane Otto of November 2016, rebuilding 20 bridges and 211 km of rural roads for ₡18,500 million.

metric.name: Priority reconstruction works concluded

secondMetric.name: Investment in the priority works

source.publisher: Government of Costa Rica, Presidencia de la República press release, republished by ReliefWeb (UN OCHA)

records.limits: The source is the government's own completion announcement; the original presidencia.go.cr page now returns 404 and the text survives in ReliefWeb's republication, which names the Government of Costa Rica as source. Completion is measured against the government's own list of 65 priority works, not against total damage: the same government estimated recovery needs at about ₡130,000 million, so ₡18,500 million is a fraction of the recovery and the record shows the priority tranche only. The started year is computed from the release's '17 months' and is not stated directly. The remaining work, a bridge over the Zapote river, was delayed by expropriation. Nothing here shows whether the rebuilt bridges and roads were built to a higher standard or maintained; the Contraloría has reported maintenance gaps on emergency-fund projects, but its document server refused connections today and that finding is not relied on.

pattern.mechanism: The CNE, which holds the national emergency fund and the declared emergency plan, contracted the state electricity and telecom utility as a single builder for the priority works instead of tendering each bridge, and coordinated it with the public works ministry and five municipalities.
preconditions: A standing emergency fund and a legal emergency declaration that unlocks direct contracting
A state enterprise with engineering crews and plant spread across the country
A short, costed list of priority works agreed in the emergency plan
pattern.travelled: Using a state utility as the reconstruction contractor recurs in Costa Rica's later emergencies; it travels only where such a utility exists and is trusted, and it concentrates risk if that enterprise is overstretched.

records.title: Contingent disaster credit with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option
records.claim: On 21 April 2020, five days after its second World Bank disaster-risk loan with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option became effective, Guatemala's government decided to withdraw the entire US$200 million to meet the fiscal shock of COVID-19, and the loan was fully disbursed. A first such credit of US$85 million, approved in 2009, had been drawn in 2010 after the Pacaya eruption and Tropical Storm Agatha.

metric.name: Contingent credit withdrawn in full (CAT DDO II)

secondMetric.name: Days from loan effectiveness to the decision to withdraw the full loan

source.publisher: World Bank Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review ICRR0024053, Guatemala DRM DPL with CAT DDO II (P159710)

records.limits: Both numbers are on page 2 of the 18-page IEG review PDF ('The loan was fully disbursed'; 'On 21 April 2020 (just five days after the project became effective), the Government decided to withdraw the entire loan'). The US$85 million first credit, its approval on 14 April 2009 (the started year) and its 2010 drawdown are from the World Bank's 2019 Program Document for the same operation (documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/977151559008837975/pdf/Guatemala-Second-Disaster-Risk-Management-Development-Policy-Loan.pdf, PDF pages 25 and 48), not from the IEG review. The money is a World Bank loan: the Guatemalan delivery is arranging it, legislating it and drawing it, and the same documents show how fragile that was. There was no contingent instrument in place for the June 2018 Fuego eruption, when 'in the absence of any other financial instrument' Congress fast-tracked an unrelated budget-support loan (Program Document page 11); total resources available for disasters were under 0.1 percent of GDP in 2017 (page 25); the second credit took a year to become effective because of conflict between the executive and Congress; and the DRM law it supported was not adopted (IEG review page 17). The withdrawal shows liquidity arrived fast, not that it was spent well; the review notes the bank could no longer supervise once the line was drawn.

pattern.mechanism: The finance ministry pre-negotiated a contingent credit line tied to a declared state of calamity, so that a declaration released money within days instead of waiting for a new loan through Congress, and layered parametric insurance and a contingent IDB line on top under a 2018 disaster risk financing strategy.
preconditions: A legal state-of-calamity declaration that can serve as the drawdown trigger
Congressional approval of the credit before the shock, which is where Guatemala lost a year
A finance ministry with a disaster risk financing strategy and budget tags to track the spending
pattern.travelled: CAT DDOs are used across Latin America (Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica, Guatemala); Guatemala's sequence shows the instrument lapsing between uses unless it is renewed before the next disaster.

records.title: National COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: From its first dose on 9 February 2021 to the end of 2023, Peru's national COVID-19 vaccination campaign administered 91.3 million doses and completed the primary series for 28.7 million people, 87 per 100 population, with 22.2 million boosted.

metric.name: Persons with a completed primary series

secondMetric.name: Persons with a completed primary series per 100 population

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 vaccination data (country-reported)

records.limits: WHO publishes what Peru's Ministry of Health reports, so the count is the country's administrative record, not a serosurvey; the CSV is machine-readable and the Peru row carries DATE_UPDATED 2023-12-29. Doses and persons are cumulative and do not show timeliness: vaccination came after Peru had already recorded one of the world's highest COVID-19 death rates, so the campaign evidences recovery capacity, not preparedness that prevented the first waves. Coverage was uneven: the ministry's own 11 December 2021 release, when 70 percent of the target population had two doses, named Madre de Dios, Puno and Ucayali below 50 percent. In January 2023 the ministry reported 1,964,490 doses close to expiry in its central warehouse. Per-100 figures use WHO's population denominator, not the national target population.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Health ran a national campaign through its own clinics plus mass sites and age-tiered scheduling, and tied access to indoor public spaces to a vaccination card from December 2021 to push the late adopters.
preconditions: Advance purchase contracts and a central cold-chain warehouse (CENARES)
A national immunization register that can count doses by person
Regional health directorates able to staff mass sites and outreach
pattern.travelled: The same campaign model ran across the region; Peru's coverage outpaced most neighbours, but the gap between Lima and the Amazon regions is the part that recurs everywhere.

records.title: Secretaría de Emergencia Nacional response to the 2019 floods
records.claim: By 29 May 2019, Paraguay's Secretaría de Emergencia Nacional had assisted 62,521 of the 65,000 families affected by the flash floods of March to May 2019 across 14 departments, delivering 1.5 million kg of food, 150,000 roofing sheets and 110,000 plywood boards.

metric.name: Flood-affected families assisted

source.publisher: Government of Paraguay (Secretaría de Emergencia Nacional) press release, republished by ReliefWeb (UN OCHA)

records.limits: Both the numerator and the 65,000 denominator are the government's own counts, published by the agency that did the work, and nobody independent checked them; the text is read on ReliefWeb's republication because sen.gov.py did not answer a scripted request today. Assistance is relief in kind (food, props, sheets and boards for self-repair), not reconstruction, resettlement or risk reduction, and the release gives no timing, so it cannot show how fast families were reached. Some assistance in the Chaco was delivered with the First Lady's office. Repeated flooding of the same Asunción riverside settlements shows the relief cycle does not reduce exposure.

pattern.mechanism: The national emergency secretariat, holding its own emergency fund, procured food and building materials centrally and distributed them department by department against a household count, with shelters in Asunción run alongside civil-society groups.
preconditions: A national emergency fund that can be drawn without a new appropriation
Stockpiles or framework contracts for food and roofing material
Municipal and departmental lists of affected households
pattern.travelled: Relief-in-kind against a household count is the common Latin American model; it closes the response gap but leaves recovery and exposure to other agencies.

records.title: National COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: From its first dose on 17 February 2021 to the end of 2023, El Salvador's national COVID-19 vaccination campaign administered 11.5 million doses and completed the primary series for 4.4 million people, 68 per 100 population.

metric.name: Persons with a completed primary series

secondMetric.name: Persons with a completed primary series per 100 population

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 vaccination data (country-reported)

records.limits: WHO republishes the Ministry of Health's administrative count; the El Salvador row carries DATE_UPDATED 2023-12-29 and no independent coverage survey is cited. A third of the population never completed the primary series and only 29 per 100 received a booster, so the delivery is national in reach but partial; Costa Rica (86) and Peru (87) completed more in the same file. The cumulative count does not show the campaign's early speed, which is its usual selling point, and that speed is not evidenced here. The government's covid19.gob.sv dashboard did not answer a scripted request and the PAHO country profile returned 403 in an earlier pass, so no national publication was read. The issue-47 rejection of this lead was on publisher_metric; the WHO file is the new evidence that fixes it.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Health vaccinated through mass sites and the public clinic network after securing early supply, and published a running national count.
preconditions: Early vaccine supply contracts or donations
A small territory and dense road network that make mass sites reachable
An immunization register that counts persons as well as doses
pattern.travelled: The mass-site model travelled across Central America; El Salvador's case shows that a fast start does not by itself carry coverage past two thirds.

records.title: Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme
records.claim: The UK's Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme, which started in March 2020, had 8.9 million jobs on furlough at its peak on 8 May 2020 and supported 11.7 million jobs from 1.3 million employers before it closed on 30 September 2021.

metric.name: Jobs on furlough at the first-wave peak

secondMetric.name: Jobs supported at any time over the life of the scheme

source.publisher: HM Revenue and Customs, Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme statistics: 16 December 2021

records.limits: HMRC is reporting on a scheme it ran, from claims data, and the counts are jobs (employments), not people: one person furloughed from two jobs counts twice. The release dates the scheme's start as March 2020 and its daily series from 23 March 2020; the announcement date (20 March 2020) and the opening of the claims portal in April 2020 are not on this page, so the speed reading rests on the peak falling on 8 May 2020, about seven weeks after the series begins. The release says nothing about cost, deadweight (jobs that would have survived anyway) or fraud and error, which HMRC and the National Audit Office reported separately, and it cannot show whether furlough preserved jobs or delayed their loss: 1.16 million jobs were still on furlough when it closed. A new scheme built in weeks under extreme pressure says little about how fast British rules change in normal times.

pattern.mechanism: The Treasury designed a wage subsidy covering 80 percent of a furloughed employee's pay and HMRC paid it to employers through the PAYE Real Time Information payroll system it already ran, so a new programme reached millions of jobs within weeks.
preconditions: A tax authority already receiving each employer's payroll in real time
Borrowing capacity to fund an open-ended subsidy
Willingness to accept fraud and deadweight in exchange for speed
pattern.travelled: Germany and France extended short-time work schemes that already existed in law; the UK built one from nothing on top of its payroll data, as Australia did with JobKeeper.

records.title: Activité partielle in the 2020 crisis
records.claim: France scaled its short-time work scheme (activité partielle) from an industrial instrument into an economy-wide one in the spring of 2020, placing 8.4 million employees on it at the April 2020 peak and 11.3 million at some point between March 2020 and December 2021.

metric.name: Employees placed on activité partielle at the peak

secondMetric.name: Employees with at least one hour of activité partielle, March 2020 to December 2021

source.publisher: Unédic, Activité partielle : état des lieux et perspectives (28 February 2022)

records.limits: Unédic is a private-law association run jointly by the employer and union confederations that manages unemployment insurance under a statutory mandate; it is not a statistics office, and this is a signed analytical study (Oana Calavrezo) in which it reports on a programme it co-financed at about one third: 14.4 billion euros in 2020 and 2021 (11.5 billion of spending and 2.9 billion of forgone receipts), more than half of its deficit in those years. The counts are Unédic's own calculations on the payment agency's claims data (ASP, Extranet Activité partielle, data at 17 January 2022, de-duplicated), stated in the full report linked from the page; the December 2021 months were provisional at that date. The labour ministry's statistics service (DARES) publishes the official series but its pages refused automated access on the retrieval date. The scheme existed before the crisis; what changed was its rules and scale, which the page describes as a change of scale 'in a few days' in the spring of 2020 without dating each decree. The count is of employees placed on the scheme, including long-term partial activity (APLD), not of jobs saved, and 45 percent of those placed on it only used it in the first lockdown. Cost per job and deadweight are not shown.

pattern.mechanism: The state widened eligibility and raised the compensation rate of an existing short-time work scheme by decree, and the state and Unédic paid employers for hours not worked, so firms could cut hours instead of jobs.
preconditions: A short-time work scheme already in law with an employer claims channel
A jointly managed unemployment insurance fund able to share the cost
Fiscal room to fund roughly a billion euros a week at the peak
pattern.travelled: The German Kurzarbeit model, which France's scheme resembles, did the same work in 2008-2009 and again in 2020; the existing legal channel is what let both pay within weeks.

records.title: Expanded Child Tax Credit of 2021, and its lapse
records.claim: The American Rescue Plan, passed in March 2021, expanded the Child Tax Credit and made it payable monthly, and on 15 July 2021 the IRS paid roughly 15 billion dollars to families of nearly 60 million children; Congress did not extend the expansion beyond 2021.

metric.name: Eligible children in families paid in the first monthly payment

secondMetric.name: Paid in the first monthly payment

source.publisher: US Department of the Treasury, press release of 15 July 2021

records.limits: The source is the Treasury announcing its own first payment, rounded ('nearly', 'roughly'), not an audited count. The four-month interval from the March 2021 law to the July payment is derived from the release's 'passed in March' and its date. The expansion was legislated for 2021 only and lapsed when Congress declined to extend it, so 'dismantled' records a decision not to continue rather than a repeal. The loss is documented by the Census Bureau, not by this source: in Poverty in the United States: 2022 (https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2023/demo/p60-280.html) the Supplemental Poverty Measure child poverty rate more than doubled, from 5.2 percent in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022, and other programmes also expired in that year, so not all of the rise is the credit. Families the IRS could not find through prior tax filings were missed by the automatic payments.

pattern.mechanism: Congress turned an annual tax credit into a monthly payment and the IRS paid it automatically from prior-year tax returns, reaching most families within four months without a new application system.
preconditions: A tax authority holding recent returns and bank details for most families
A legislative majority willing to pass a large temporary expansion
A political settlement to make it permanent, which was missing
pattern.travelled: Child allowances paid monthly are permanent in Canada and much of Europe; the US case shows a temporary expansion can be delivered quickly and lost as quickly when its legal basis is time-limited.

records.title: Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, the free foodgrain response to COVID-19
records.claim: India's Department of Food and Public Distribution, acting on the Garib Kalyan package announced in March 2020, allocated about 121 lakh tonnes of extra free foodgrains to States on 30 March 2020, and States distributed 37.5 lakh tonnes covering about 75 crore beneficiaries in each of April and May 2020.

metric.name: Beneficiaries covered by the extra free grain each month

secondMetric.name: Foodgrains distributed in Phase I, April to June 2020

source.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, release 1643542 (5 August 2020), from Food Corporation of India reports

records.limits: The figures are the ministry's own, compiled from what States reported to the Food Corporation of India, and are not an audit of what reached households; distribution counts at ration shops are known to include leakage. The scheme worked by adding 5 kg per person to the existing National Food Security Act ration lists, so people outside those lists, including many migrant workers stranded in the 2020 lockdown, were not covered by this channel. The extra entitlement was extended repeatedly and ended in December 2022, when the Cabinet instead made the regular NFSA ration free from January 2023. Speed is read from the release's dates (allocation on 30 March 2020, distribution from April) rather than a timestamped series.

pattern.mechanism: The central government doubled the grain ration by order and pushed the extra stock from Food Corporation of India depots through the existing ration-shop network, so no new eligibility system had to be built.
preconditions: Large public grain stocks already held in central depots
A national ration-card register and shop network covering about 80 crore people
States able to lift and distribute stock within weeks
pattern.travelled: In-kind rations through an existing public distribution system are hard to copy where no such stock and register exist; cash transfers did the same job elsewhere.

records.title: Targeted Economic Support Scheme (TESS)
records.claim: The Central Bank of the UAE launched the Targeted Economic Support Scheme in March 2020, combining a zero-cost liquidity facility with loan deferrals and capital relief, and by 24 September 2020 more than 300,000 individuals, close to 10,000 SMEs and more than 1,500 private corporates had benefited from the facility.

metric.name: Individuals who benefited from the TESS zero-cost liquidity facility

secondMetric.name: SMEs that benefited from the TESS zero-cost liquidity facility

source.publisher: Central Bank of the UAE, press release 'CBUAE Governor reviews TESS Program and Systemic Stability with Banks CEO's' (24 September 2020)

records.limits: The figures are a central bank press release about its own scheme, rounded ('more than', 'close to'), with no breakdown of amounts or of who would have received relief anyway. The March 2020 start, the extension the following month and the run to 30 June 2022 are stated in the central bank's UAE MSMEs Business Survey Report 2020 (page 10, https://centralbank.ae/media/rtdlng34/cbuae-msme-survey-report-2020-en.pdf), not in this release, and the central bank's web pages sit behind a bot check while its PDFs open. Benefiting from a liquidity facility means a bank passed on a deferral or cheaper credit; it does not show firms or jobs saved. Banks surveyed in that report counted 7,751 MSME customers helped by TESS in 2020, a different measure from this one.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank lent to banks at zero cost against collateral and relaxed capital and liquidity buffers on condition that they defer repayments for affected borrowers, so relief reached households and firms through existing bank relationships.
preconditions: A banking sector holding most household and SME credit
A central bank with authority to set conditional liquidity and capital relief
Fiscal and reserve strength under the currency peg
pattern.travelled: Most central banks ran deferral and liquidity schemes in 2020; the conditional zero-cost facility is the UAE's variant.

records.title: Phased exemption of enterprise social insurance contributions, 2020
records.claim: China's human resources ministry, finance ministry and tax administration let provinces exempt or halve employer pension, unemployment and work-injury contributions from February 2020 under a notice dated 20 February, and exemptions, reductions, deferrals and rate cuts together reduced contributions by 1.54 trillion yuan between February and the end of 2020.

metric.name: Contributions reduced by exemption, reduction, deferral and rate cuts, February to December 2020

secondMetric.name: Enterprises receiving unemployment insurance job-stabilisation refunds in 2020

source.publisher: National Development and Reform Commission, Employment Department, page of 27 January 2021, republished from China News Service

records.limits: The figure is a government figure republished by the NDRC Employment Department from China News Service (中国新闻网), which the page names as its source; the page does not name the originating ministry or event, and the figure does not appear in the human resources ministry's 2020 statistical bulletin. It adds exemptions, reductions, deferrals and rate cuts together, and the rate cuts include reductions in force before the February 2020 notice, and a deferral is postponed rather than forgiven, so 1.54 trillion yuan overstates the relief. The rule itself is dated by the notice (Ren She Bu Fa 2020 No. 11, 2020-02-20, https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2020-02/21/content_5481861.htm), which let provinces exempt small firms for up to five months and halve large firms' contributions for up to three. The cost landed on the funds: the same page reports 2020 revenue of 5.02 trillion yuan against spending of 5.75 trillion. This is relief for enterprises that pay contributions, not for informal workers.

pattern.mechanism: Three central agencies used the Social Insurance Law's authority to suspend the employer share of contributions by notice, and the tax administration, which collects them, applied it from the next collection cycle.
preconditions: Contributions collected centrally by the tax administration
Pension fund balances large enough to absorb a year of lost revenue
Central authority to change contribution rules by notice rather than law
pattern.travelled: Contribution holidays were used widely in 2020; China's was large because contributions are a large share of labour cost, and its cost was a fund deficit rather than a budget line.

records.title: Business Finland disruption funding, 2020
records.claim: Finland redirected Business Finland, its innovation funding agency, to pay emergency development grants to firms hit by the epidemic, starting from a 700 million euro allocation in the supplementary budget adopted on 26 March 2020, and by 2 September 2020 it had allocated about 912 million euros to 18,770 projects out of 28,715 that applied.

metric.name: Business Finland disruption funding allocated

secondMetric.name: Projects funded

source.publisher: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, press release of 2 September 2020

records.limits: The ministry is reporting its own agency's grants, and an allocation is a decision, not a payment. The 26 March 2020 supplementary budget and the 700 million euro allocation come from a separate government release (https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-//1410877/valtion-rahoitusta-yrityksille-koronavirustilanteessa-vahvistetaan-yritystukiin-miljardi-euroa), not from the source page, and neither page explains how allocations reached 912 million euros against the initial 700 million. Using an R&D agency for emergency aid was fast but loosely targeted: the grants were for 'development' (79 million euros for preliminary analyses and 832 million for development funding), and later reports of recoveries and suspected misuse are not on either page. Neither page shows whether the firms survived or what share of the grants was later recovered.

pattern.mechanism: Rather than build a new aid channel, the government gave its innovation agency new grant instruments and money by supplementary budget, so applications could open within days through an existing online system.
preconditions: An agency already running an online grant system that reached most SMEs
Parliament able to pass a supplementary budget within days
Tolerance for weaker screening than normal R&D funding
pattern.travelled: Several countries used existing enterprise agencies for 2020 grants; the Finnish case shows the trade between speed and targeting when the agency's purpose is innovation, not relief.

records.title: Partial and flexible unemployment subsidy, 2020-2021
records.claim: Uruguay's labour ministry created partial and flexible unemployment-subsidy modalities by resolution after the health emergency of 13 March 2020, and the social security bank (BPS) paid 12,773 beneficiaries under them in April 2020, while total unemployment-subsidy beneficiaries rose from 45,937 in February to a record 185,769 in May.

metric.name: Beneficiaries under the new partial and flexible modalities in their first month

secondMetric.name: Total unemployment-subsidy beneficiaries at the 2020 peak

source.publisher: Banco de Previsión Social, Asesoría General en Seguridad Social, Comentarios de Seguridad Social No. 85 (March 2022), Impacto del COVID-19 en el subsidio por desempleo

records.limits: BPS is analysing a benefit it pays, from its own administrative records, and the numbers are inside a PDF (Cuadro 2 on page 6 and Cuadro 4 on page 13 of the file). Most of the surge went through the ordinary subsidy for total suspension, which already existed; the new modalities, set by labour ministry resolutions 143/20, 163/20, 233/20 and 1024/20 (partial) and 2225/20, 21/21 and 97/21 (flexible), peaked at 30,221 beneficiaries in June 2020 and fell to 10,549 by December 2021. The record evidences rules changed and paid within weeks, not jobs kept: a beneficiary count is a monthly stock, and the report does not estimate how many of those workers returned to their jobs. The end date of the special regime is not in this source.

pattern.mechanism: The labour ministry used its resolution power to open the unemployment subsidy to workers whose hours were cut rather than suspended, and BPS paid it through the claims channel employers already used.
preconditions: An unemployment insurance law that let the ministry create special regimes by resolution
A single social security agency holding employer and wage records
Employers able to file partial suspensions online
pattern.travelled: Partial unemployment benefits are the short-time work idea under another name; Uruguay's version was built by resolution in weeks because the legal hook for special regimes already existed.

records.title: Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia, the COVID-19 household transfer
records.claim: Chile's Congress created the Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia by Ley 21.230, published on 16 May 2020, and the Ministry of Social Development and Family issued payments to 3,419,351 households in 2020 and to 8,374,718 households in 2021, before the programme ended in 2021.

metric.name: Households issued an IFE payment

secondMetric.name: Households issued an IFE payment in the first year

source.publisher: Ministerio de Desarrollo Social y Familia, Subsecretaría de Servicios Sociales, Monitoreo y Seguimiento Oferta Pública 2021: Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia

records.limits: The ministry is reporting on its own programme, and the counts sit in a six-page PDF monitoring sheet (component table on page 4); no Contraloría audit was consulted. The unit is households in the Registro Social de Hogares to which a payment was issued in the year, which is a registry unit and not a census household, and a household paid in several months counts once per year as far as the sheet shows. The sheet gives annual totals only, so it does not show how many weeks passed between the law and the first payment; the law's publication date (16 May 2020) comes from the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional record of Ley 21.230 (https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/navegar?idNorma=1145400), which also shows Ley 21.251 amending it on 3 August 2020. Initial budget execution in 2021 was 2,024 percent of the budget law (page 2), which shows the scale of in-year change but also that the programme ran outside the normal budget process. The monthly ministry reports that would carry the week-by-week roll-out (desarrollosocialyfamilia.gob.cl/storage/docs/ife/) returned HTTP 500 on 2 October 2026. Spending of about 17.0 trillion pesos in 2021 says nothing about targeting errors or the poverty effect, and a transfer that ended in 2021 does not show that Chilean rules change quickly in general.

pattern.mechanism: Congress legislated a time-limited cash benefit keyed to an existing social registry, then amended it as the pandemic went on, and the ministry paid through bank accounts and in-person collection to every registered household that met the income test.
preconditions: A national social registry (Registro Social de Hogares) covering most households before the shock
Fiscal space and a legislature able to pass and amend a benefit law within weeks
Payment rails reaching households with and without bank accounts
pattern.travelled: Registry-keyed emergency transfers were the common Latin American response in 2020, from Guatemala's Bono Familia to Panama's Vale Digital. Chile's version differs in scale relative to its registry, and in being repeatedly widened by law rather than by decree.

records.title: Central Bank of Kenya emergency loan restructuring measures
records.claim: The Central Bank of Kenya announced emergency measures on 18 and 24 March 2020 that let banks restructure loans performing on 2 March 2020, and by the end of February 2021, days before the measures expired on 2 March 2021, loans of Ksh 1.7 trillion, 57 percent of the banking sector's gross loans, had been restructured.

metric.name: Loans restructured under the emergency measures, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Restructured loans still outstanding when the measures expired

source.publisher: Central Bank of Kenya, press release: Expiry of Emergency Measures on Restructuring of Loans for Bank Borrowers (23 March 2021)

records.limits: The regulator is grading its own measure: the release calls it highly effective and gives no independent evaluation, and the figures are a one-page press release PDF, not a supervisory dataset. Restructuring is a forbearance rule, not new money, and restructured loans can hide losses: the share says nothing about how many restructured loans later defaulted, beyond the release's own statement that over 95 percent of the Ksh 569.3 billion still outstanding was being repaid on restructured terms. The cumulative 57 percent counts amounts, not borrowers, and includes loans restructured more than once if banks reported them so. The speed evidence is a separate CBK release: the Monetary Policy Committee statement of 29 July 2020 (https://www.centralbank.go.ke/uploads/mpc_press_release/603807985_MPC%20Press%20Release%20-%20Meeting%20of%20July%2029%202020.pdf) reports KES 844.4 billion, 29 percent of the loan book, restructured by the end of June 2020, the same release that reports the gross NPL ratio at 13.1 percent. One temporary financial-sector rule does not show how fast Kenyan public programmes change in general.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank changed loan classification and provisioning rules by circular within a week of the first case, letting banks extend repayment, grant moratoria and waive fees on loans performing before the shock, and set a fixed expiry date after which standard classification resumed.
preconditions: A central bank with direct supervisory authority over loan classification
Banks capitalised enough to carry restructured loans for a year
A dated cut-off (loans performing on 2 March 2020) that kept pre-existing bad loans out
pattern.travelled: Time-bound restructuring windows were used by many central banks in 2020; the fixed expiry and the published cumulative-versus-outstanding figures are the part that makes Kenya's version auditable.

records.title: Conditional cash transfer shock response, and its suspension after 2022
records.claim: Honduras widened its national conditional cash transfer during COVID-19 and Hurricanes Eta and Iota, from 1,153,069 beneficiaries in 2019 to 1,528,030 in 2020, and paid emergency top-ups to 24,891 households outside the roster in late 2020, but after the 2022 reorganisation of the social protection sector payments paused, rural payments resumed only in December 2022 and urban payments only in August 2025, after a three-year suspension.

metric.name: Suspension of urban CCT payments after the 2022 transition

secondMetric.name: Beneficiaries of social safety net programmes at the 2020 peak

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Honduras Social Protection Integration Project (P152057)

records.limits: The publisher financed the project (US$30 million, then a US$70 million additional financing in June 2021) and rates it Substantial on efficacy; the figures are in a PDF (beneficiary counts and the top-up figure on page 19, paragraphs 31 and 33; the payment pause on page 14, paragraph 14; the three-year urban suspension in paragraph 39). The ICR states explicitly that the 1,528,030 peak (cumulative enrollment) and the 922,832 final-year caseload are distinct measures that should not be compared directly, and attributes the lower figure to a compressed implementation window, not a reversal of reach; the Borrower's completion report summarised in the annex gives 961,339 beneficiaries at closing (page 58), 62 percent of target. The record therefore does not use the final-year caseload as its metric: the erosion it documents is the payment pause, which the ICR does state (metric, the three-year urban suspension, paragraph 39, PDF page 21): payments stopped during the 2022 transition to SEDESOL and the Red Solidaria, with rural payments resuming in December 2022 and urban payments after a three-year suspension. The emergency top-up was small (24,891 households) and the source gives no elapsed time for it beyond late 2020. The 2019 to 2020 rise mixes horizontal expansion with routine enrolment. A change of government that redesigns a programme is a political choice, not only a loss of capacity.

pattern.mechanism: The social protection ministry used an existing conditional cash transfer and its registry to add vulnerable households and pay top-ups after COVID-19 and two hurricanes, financed by an additional World Bank credit; a new administration then moved the programme to a new ministry and new targeting rules, and payments stopped until the new architecture could pay.
preconditions: A standing transfer programme with a beneficiary registry before the shock
External finance that could be added within a year
Implementing institutions that survive a change of government, which is the precondition that failed here
pattern.travelled: Honduras published a shock-response protocol for the transfer (PROMESA-PSA, Ministerial Agreement 159-SEDESOL-2025, 9 December 2025) built on the 2020 top-up. The lesson the ICR draws is that institutional reform can disrupt delivery more than the external shocks did.

records.title: Food relief from the national reserve during the July 2021 lockdown
records.claim: After the cabinet ordered a lockdown on 14 July 2021, Rwanda's government released part of the national food reserves on 15 July, and between 18 and 30 July local governments delivered about 7,000 tonnes of food door to door to more than 327,000 families in Kigali and eight districts, including 103,000 families not on the initial list.

metric.name: Families receiving food relief

secondMetric.name: Families added beyond the initial list

source.publisher: Ministry of Local Government (MINALOC), news: How Government supported families with food relief during 3rd lockdown

records.limits: The source is the implementing ministry's own news item, written as a success story with quotes from a beneficiary and the minister, and the figures are rounded ('more than 327 thousand', 'around seven thousand tones'); there is no audit, no list of families, and the page shows no publication date. It covers one 15-day lockdown in Kigali and eight of Rwanda's 30 districts, in kind rather than cash, and says nothing about who was missed, the quality of targeting or the cost. The four-day lag from the cabinet decision (14 July) to the start of deliveries (18 July) is the speed evidence, and it rests on the ministry's own dating. Earlier lockdown relief in 2020 is not covered here. One well-run emergency distribution, in a state with unusually dense local administration and mandatory community structures, does not show that Rwandan rules change quickly in general.

pattern.mechanism: The cabinet's lockdown decision was paired the next day with a release from the national food reserve; sector and cell officials drew up household lists, opened a channel for unlisted families to claim by toll-free line, SMS and social media, and delivered door to door with youth volunteers.
preconditions: A physical national strategic food reserve
Local administration down to the cell and village level able to list households within days
A claims channel so the initial list could be corrected during delivery
pattern.travelled: Lockdown food distribution was widespread in 2020 and 2021 and often failed on targeting; the claim-in channel that added roughly a third to the list is the transferable element.

records.title: Private Finance Initiative and PF2, and their abolition
records.claim: HM Treasury's Private Finance Initiative signed on average 55 contracts a year between 1997 and 2010 and left 704 current PFI and PF2 projects with a capital value of £57 billion at 31 March 2018, after signings fell to an average of nine a year after May 2010 and the Chancellor announced at Budget 2018 that the government would no longer use PF2 for new projects.

metric.name: Current PFI and PF2 projects (in operation or construction)

secondMetric.name: Average PFI contracts signed per year, 1997 to 2010 (peak era; 9 a year after May 2010)

source.publisher: HM Treasury and Infrastructure and Projects Authority, Private Finance Initiative and Private Finance 2 projects: 2018 summary data

records.limits: This is a dismantling by decision of the procurement route, not of the assets: the 704 contracts keep running, with £188.35 billion of forecast unitary charges over the next 30 years, so the record shows a national collaboration model closed to new deals rather than a lost stock of hospitals and schools. The decline started well before abolition (an average of 55 signings a year from 1997 to 2010 against nine a year after May 2010), and PF2, introduced in 2012 'in response to widespread concerns about value for money', was used only six times. A hostile reviewer would say PFI is evidence of joint delivery at scale and of poor value for money at once: the scale figure says nothing about whether the risk transfer paid off, and the Carillion liquidation hit two PF2 projects.
